For, says *Albertus Magnus* <note>Albertus Magnus (c. 1200–1280) was a Dominican friar and polymath. *Metamorphosis* <note>original Latin: *morphosi*. Likely referring to the transformation of substances.</note>, the *Tincture of the Philosophers* <note>original: *Philosophorum tinctura*. A mythological prize used here as a metaphor for the Philosopher's Stone or the ultimate secret of transmutation.</note>.

### Hieronymus Reusner’s Dedication

...the most generous lord and patron, I could find none more suitable than this gentleman himself, especially since he still holds this art <note>The "art" refers to alchemy and the Paracelsian medical philosophy discussed in the preceding pages.</note> in high regard. For I cannot sufficiently praise, much less give thanks for, the great kindnesses the gentleman showed me when I was in Lauingen <note>A town in Bavaria which, at the time, was a significant center for learning and printing.</note> a year ago. 

In addition, I was prompted in no small part by the great friendship I perceived and clearly noted between the gentleman and the honorable and highly learned Mr. *Nicolaus Reusner*, Doctor of both Laws <note>original Latin: *Doctor utriusque iuris*, meaning he held a doctorate in both Civil and Canon law.</note> and Rector of the school, my dearly beloved cousin.

Therefore, my diligent and sole request to the Doctor is that he would favorably and kindly accept this beautiful maiden *Pandora*, and be her *Epimetheus* <note>In the context of this book, "Pandora" represents the box of alchemical secrets, and "Epimetheus" (the brother of Prometheus) acts as the guardian or interpreter who receives her. Reusner is asking his patron to protect the book from critics.</note>, so that she might not fall into the dens of thieves <note>original German: *Mörder-Gruben*, literally "murder-pits," a metaphorical term for a place of corruption or hostile criticism.</note> in these times, when almost no faith remains, even among trusted friends. I further most humbly pray the gentleman that he would continue to support me and my *Medical Studies* <note>original Latin: *Studia Medica*.</note> as he has done until now.

# Or the Noblest Gift of God.

I shall be permitted to trust further in my **experience** <note>original: *Experientz*</note> and the righteous writings of the wise, rather than the *imagination* of another. Moreover, the often-mentioned dear, ancient, and true **philosophers** <note>original: *Philosophi*; a term used specifically for practitioners of the alchemical art</note> did not have such great **expenses** <note>original: *Sumptus*</note> to build such beautiful, artistic furnaces and magnificent **laboratories** <note>original: *Laboratoria*</note> as is the custom now; instead, they devoted themselves to one small furnace in a quiet place and attended to it. The multitude of many furnaces indicates manifold **labors** <note>original: *Labores*</note> and diverse matters, whereas all writings unanimously **agree** <note>original: *concordiren*</note> that our art does not consist in the essence of many things, just as <term>Hermes</term> <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of alchemy to whom the *Emerald Tablet* is attributed</note> clearly speaks of this. Therefore, no beginning student need concern himself with many furnaces and **laboratories**; a single small furnace, in which he can manage his **degrees** <note>original: *Gradus*; the specific levels of heat—traditionally four—required at different stages of the alchemical process</note> is quite enough; let him place it in a location where there is no cause for concern regarding fire hazards, so that the Devil, as a hateful enemy, does not create one commotion after another. To this [furnace], let him add a [vessel], fill it with sand or <unclear>a</unclear>shes, and place his small glass within it; he must not take it out until he sees the entire **mass** <note>original: *massam*</note> transformed into a beautiful blood-red color, which is a sign of his **harvest** <note>original: *Ernde*; the successful completion of the Great Work, resulting in the red Philosopher's Stone</note>.

->Heinrich von Batsdorff.<-

# PANDORA,
<meta>catchword: Also</meta>

(dd) If anyone should wish to doubt the certainty of this art, let him read the many books of the ancient Philosophers <note>The author refers to the long lineage of alchemists and natural scientists from antiquity whose works formed the basis of medieval science</note> grounded in reason and experience; as they are credible witnesses, they are not to be mistrusted in their art. Moreover, whoever does not believe them is not to be argued with, as he is one who contradicts the **Principles** <note>original: "Principia," meaning the fundamental axioms or laws of a science</note> and first causes; for the **deaf** and **mute** cannot speak. I have said that the art is true. For what advantage should all other things in the world have over the metals? Why should we unjustly exclude metals alone from the **Creator’s** general **blessing of multiplication** <note>This refers to the biblical command in Genesis to "be fruitful and multiply." Alchemists believed that minerals, like plants and animals, possessed a "seed" and the potential to grow if placed in the right conditions</note>, by refusing to acknowledge that they possess a seed? For Holy Scripture testifies that such a blessing was implanted in and shared with all created things from the beginning. If they have a seed, who would be so foolish as to believe they could not be increased within their own seed? In its nature, the **Alchemical Art** <note>original: "Chymistische Kunst"</note> is true; Nature is also true, but the **artist** <note>In alchemical texts, the "artist" is the practitioner or chemist performing the experiment</note> is seldom true and right. There is one Nature, and thus there is one Art, but there are many kinds of artists.

He asserts that while the laws of Nature and Alchemy are constant, the failures of the craft lie with the unskilled practitioners, not the Art itself.</summary>

<margin>(c) But if the heat is more vehement than is proper, this spiritual nature is struck as if by the hammer of death; from active it becomes passive, and from spiritual it becomes corporeal—namely, a useless red precipitate. This is because, when kept in its proper heat, the color becomes a raven’s black <note>original: "corvinæ nigredinis." Therefore, the entire hollow of the glass vessel will be tinted with a golden color. Only make haste slowly <note>original: "festina lente," a classic alchemical maxim advising the practitioner to avoid rushing the delicate process</note>, and yet continue a sufficiently strong fire. Steer your ship like a skilled pilot between Scylla and Charybdis <note>In Greek mythology, these were two monsters on either side of a narrow strait; here, they represent the danger of using either too much or too little heat</note>, if you desire to gain the riches of both the Indies <note>A metaphor for the ultimate material and spiritual wealth produced by the Philosopher's Stone</note>. At times you will see what look like small islands, sending out multicolored spikes and parasols in the waves and at the sides of the vessel; these will soon dissolve, and others will rise up.</margin>

# Or the Noblest Gift of GOD.

Naming and comparing this work specifically to a stone is done primarily for this reason: because the Material <term>Materia; the raw substance used in the work</term> of the same in the beginning, as a Mineral <term>Minera; a primary ore</term> from the earth, is truly a stone. Furthermore, because it is hard and dry, it can be crushed and ground like a stone. # Or the Noblest Gift of God.

...most <note>The text continues from the previous page's catchword "most," likely completing the word "noblest" (German: *edelste*).</note> <term>final cause <note>original: "End-Ursache"; in Aristotelian philosophy, the *causa finalis* or the ultimate purpose for which a thing exists.</note></term> is a sign of excellence, then the Stone, which has the most perfect <note>The original text uses a macron over the 'm' in "vollkommenste," a common scribal shorthand to indicate a doubled letter.</note> final cause among those things that are purely natural, shall be the most highly esteemed of all. Man is a prince of this world, and I posit that all created beings strive to serve him, and according to their nature are collectively ready to do him good, in that they regard him as their final cause. Because this is so, the greatest good of man is the right noble final cause of the creatures here below; now, there is no greater happiness of which he is capable—if I consider him outside the state of Grace <note>The author distinguishes between spiritual salvation (grace) and earthly well-being.</note>—than health and wealth. From these two, as if from two fountains, flow all the goods that he may desire. Wealth gives him the means to satisfy all his wishes; with it, he can purchase high offices and honor to please his mind. He can possess all delights with which the senses may enjoy themselves to still their appetite and desire; likewise, health lets him taste all pleasures as far as they can extend; and therefore, ultimately, the Stone, which gives to man both the one and the other, is to be reckoned as having the noblest <term>final cause</term>, according to its excellence and perfection.

->Johann Lang.<-

# PANDORA,

[approximately] twenty years after the birth of Christ, 
the magnificent art of glassmaking arose, so that with a simple tempering <term>Temperatur</term> <note>In this context, "temperature" refers to the "tempering" or the specific proportional mixing of ingredients rather than just heat.</note> of sand, grit, ashes, and certain hard metallic juices <note>Likely referring to mineral salts or metallic oxides used as fluxes or colorants.</note>, through the power of fire, glass could be prepared to be liquid, castable, flexible, pliable, and ductile—just like a soft metal—for all kinds of utility and elegance. Then the Roman Emperor **Tiberius** intervened and banned and abolished the workshop <term>Officin</term> <note>From the Latin *officina*, meaning a workshop or laboratory.</note> of such an honorable, elegant, and useful art; indeed, as **Isidore** <note>Isidore of Seville (c. 560–636 AD), an influential scholar whose *Etymologiae* preserved many classical legends, including the story of *vitrum flexile* or flexible glass.</note> writes, he even had the master of such skill put to death.

And he did this solely for this pretext: namely, that through the rise of this art, beautiful, transparent, clear glass would in time displace pale gold and bring it into worthlessness or contempt; and thus, through this, gold would finally lose its value and esteem, bringing down all commerce, trade, merchant dealings, and industry.

Which is such a wretched and worthless reason from such a high potentate that one might well say he did not behave as a **Tiberius**, but rather—as he was commonly mocked for his habitual drunkenness—as a **Biberius** <note>original: "Biberius." A contemporary Roman pun on the Emperor’s name, Tiberius Claudius Nero, which was twisted into "Biberius Caldius Mero"—roughly translating to "the drinker of hot, undiluted wine."</note>, having fetched and drawn this idea out of a drinking glass.

<summary>This page recounts the legend of the invention of flexible glass under Emperor Tiberius, who allegedly suppressed the invention and executed its creator to prevent glass from becoming more valuable than gold. The author uses this to criticize leaders who suppress knowledge out of economic fear, mocking Tiberius with a historical pun on his drinking habits.</summary>

### The Stone is out of the four Elements. (b)

(b) In the same way, the philosophers have divided their **Stone** into these very parts: namely, into a **Body**, into a **Spirit**, and into a **Soul**. The *spiritus* <note>original Latin for spirit</note> or spirit is a life of the soul; the soul's life, however, is the spirit. Conversely, these two are the life of the body. The spirit is a knot <note>a binding link or nexus</note> of the soul and the body, by which they are bound together in the body; it is like a heavenly path that spreads the power of the soul through the entire *corpus* <note>body</note>.

You may also understand it this way: when the philosophers say that their stone is made out of a body, soul, and spirit, understand the elements of the body: the water <note>original symbol: $\nabla$</note>, the air, the fire <note>original symbol: $\Delta$</note>, and the earth. For the water is a spirit; furthermore, the air and the fire—to speak of it plainly—are a middle and prepared spirit. But the earth we do not call a spirit, but rather a *corpus* <note>body</note>, which is a mother to the other elements, in which they are planted.

...chemical water, or <term>first matter</term> <note>original: *materia prima*; the formless, primal substance from which all things are made.</note>, the metals are resolved again and dissolved from their hard, rigid, frozen bonds into their first and identical nature, just as the water of <term>Mercury</term> <note>original: *Mercurii*.</note> itself is. Therefore they say: from whatever substance a thing has its first beginning, into that same thing and with that same thing it is also brought back, so that it becomes what it was in the beginning. <note>original Latin: *Omnium enim Naturalissimum est unumquodque Eodem modo solvi quo colligatum est.*</note> For it is the most natural of all things that each thing be dissolved in the same manner in which it was bound together. For that which dissolves and that which is dissolved are of one genus and nature. <note>original Latin: *corporis soluti & aquæ solvendis natura una est, nisi quod natura corporis completa & fixa, Aquæ verò Natura incompleta & volatilis est, propterea ut natura mutet & convertat , tantum eo indiget, quod est suæ naturæ. # Or God’s Noblest Gift.

Because of this, the Philosophers said: "cook gently and with a slow fire." For a strong fire destroys the work and dissipates it; but a slow fire leads to health and generates a single substance. And as **Geber** says: A slow fire is preservative of the **natural humidity** <term>natural/radical humidity: The vital, intrinsic moisture within matter that allows for growth and flexibility; alchemists believed that if this was "burned away" by too much heat, the work would fail.</term>, or radical humidity, and is conducive to melting; but a more vehement fire is destructive to humidity.

These things being known, there still remains a doubt: how much heat of the sun is necessary and sufficient for this work; because in slow heat, just as in strong heat, many degrees can be understood. For there is that which is slower than slow, just as in strong heat, there is that which is stronger than strong. ...[as far as they] extend: for nothing makes a thing white, except by its own whiteness, and nothing makes a thing red, except by its own redness. <note>original: "nulla res dealbat nisi secundum suam albedinem, nec nulla res rubificat nisi secundum suam rubedinem." This philosophical principle suggests that a substance cannot give what it does not possess; natural gold has "goldness," but the Elixir must have a concentrated "power of coloring" far beyond the natural metal.</note> Nor does it contradict the authority of <term>Geber</term> <note>The Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, a legendary 8th-century figure considered the father of alchemy; here likely referring to the 13th-century Latin author known as Pseudo-Geber.</note> when he says in another place: "Perfect bodies do not need preparation, since they are already perfect, but only that they may be further <term>subtilized</term> <note>original: "subtilientur"; the process of making a substance more refined, volatile, or spiritually potent.</note>." Perfect metals (gold and silver) do not need this initial stage, as they lack the superfluous black and burning moisture or the unclean, coarse, and earthly dregs that imperfect metals possess. But nevertheless, the Philosophers testify enough that after their solution, their <term>calces</term> <note>original: "calces"; the fine powders resulting from the heating or "killing" of metals.</note> and their <term>Mercury</term> <note>In alchemy, Mercury represents the "spirit" or fluid principle of all metals, not merely the liquid metal we know today.</note> must be cleansed just as much as those of the imperfect metals.

# Or Noblest Gift of God.

Do not wonder how a single weak metal, which does not have the weight of a perfect metal, is returned to its true weight through the <term>medicine</term> <note>original: "medicinam"; in alchemy, the "medicine" is the Philosopher's Stone or Elixir, which was believed to "heal" or "perfect" base metals into gold.</note> when a tiny amount of that medicine is placed upon it—and so small an amount that the weight of that tiny bit cannot possibly account for the missing weight of the metal, relative to the quantity of medicine applied. This is so, as all the philosophers say, because it happens through the power of the medicine, which by its own nature, when it gives the <term>tincture</term> <note>original: "tincturam"; the transformative essence or "dye" that permeates a metal to change its properties and color.</note>, it also gives the weight of that tincture, whether in white <note>In white (albo) refers to the transformation into silver.</note> or in red <note>In red (rubeo) refers to the transformation into gold.</note>. This is something that <term>sophistic medicine</term> <note>original: "medicina sophistica"; refers to "fake" alchemy or "sophistry" that only changes the appearance or color of a metal (like a plating) without changing its inner nature or density.</note> does not do, for it only gives the appearance of color and not the true weight.

->Anonymous<-

(b) ¶ It is to be twice rectified <note>original: "Ta bis rectificandum"; "Ta" is likely a printer's contraction for "Ita" (thus) or "Hæc" (this). ->Master Johan Isaac Hollandus.<- <note>A famous, though somewhat legendary, Dutch alchemist of the 15th century whose writings were highly influential in the development of laboratory chemistry.</note>

# PANDORA

<margin>(c) This water is like the poisonous snakes of Tyre <note>original: "Schlangen Tyrus"; Tyrus or Tyrian vipers were legendary components used in the preparation of ancient universal antidotes. In alchemy, this often refers to a corrosive or "venomous" solvent.</note>, and with it the powerful <term>Theriac</term> <note>A famous medicinal "polypharmacy" compound, originally used as an antidote to poison but later considered by alchemists as a universal panacea once perfected.</note> is prepared. It is the most severe "poison of wrath"; a stronger poison cannot be imagined. For this reason, it was often sought by apothecaries, but from the moment it is transformed into the **Elixir**, no one shall be poisoned by it.</margin>

This water is called "their poison" by the Philosophers, and it is indeed a very strong poison—specifically to the **Body of Gold** <note>In alchemy, the "body" refers to the solid, metallic state of the element.</note> with which it is mixed. But as for the human body, I have never tested it myself, nor given it to another, and I do not believe that any of them <note>The philosophers/alchemists.</note> have done so.

However, concerning the **Medicine** that is made through and from this same water, it is certain that it is the highest medicine of all in the world. For it is the true **Tree of Life**, which generally satisfies the desires of all those who possess it in its proper form. For besides its healing power, which it possesses in a wonderful, miraculous way, it can penetrate even to our very origins <note>original: "Anfangen"; the fundamental elements or "first principles" from which the human body is composed.</note> from which we are composed—something no other mineral medicine can do. Even though **Paracelsus** <note>Philippus Aureolus Theophrastus Bombastus von Hohenheim (1493–1541), a Swiss physician and alchemist who argued that the purpose of alchemy was to create medicines rather than just gold.</note> [mentions] his <term>Restaurantia</term> <note>Latin: "restoratives"; substances intended to restore the body's strength.</note> and <term>Renovantia</term> <note>Latin: "renovatives"; substances intended to renew youth or health.</note>

It was their opinion that that which ascends should be named the **first sublimation** <note>original Latin: *sublimatio*; the process of a substance turning into vapor and rising when heated</note>. ...unless a friend has revealed it, it is recognized only with difficulty. For we cannot all be Geber <note>original: *Gebri*; referring to Jabir ibn Hayyan (c. 721–815), a foundational figure in alchemy</note>, nor can we all be Lully <note>original: *Lullii*; referring to Ramon Llull (c. 1232–1315), a Majorcan philosopher and credited alchemist</note>. And although Lully was a man of subtle intellect, if he had not received the art from Arnold <note>Arnold of Villanova, mentioned on the previous page</note>, he certainly would have been like the others who seek it with difficulty; indeed, even Arnold confesses to have received it from a friend.

->Michael Maier.<-
<note>Michael Maier (1568–1622) was a German physician and counselor to Rudolf II, famous for his alchemical emblems and writings.</note>

I have not said all the things that appear and are necessary in this work; for there are some things which it is not fitting to tell to men; yet I have written and depicted it until the end, or the fulfillment, although I have not seen it myself. (a)

<margin>(a)</margin> As to what moved the <term>Philosophers; in this context, the "Philosophers by Fire" or alchemists</term> to describe this art through similarities and obscure allegories, one universal reason is passed down everywhere: lest it be revealed to the foolish, the unlearned, and the impious, and lest the unworthy, in their contempt for nature, should take possession of such a great treasure. Specifically, however, I find twelve reasons: the author of the *Universal Way* <note>original: *viæ universalis*; likely a reference to a specific alchemical text or the common path of the Great Work</note> brings forward the first: Lest it be recognized and known that this science is true and entirely certain. And indeed, unless the minds of men were restrained by that uncertainty and doubt, many more would [bind] themselves in indissoluble bonds...

...[with the difficulties] of this art, especially the greedy and the arrogant, and those who burn with the lust for power. **Hamuel in *The Senior*** <note>original: *Seniore*; referring to the *De Chemia*, a text by the 10th-century author Senior Zadith (Ibn Umail)</note> alleges the second reason: That they might attribute the art to the **Glorious God**, so that He might reveal it to whom He willed, and withhold it from whom He willed. Hence **Geber** <note>original: *Gebri*; referring to Jabir ibn Hayyan (c. 721–815), a foundational figure in alchemy</note> says: Our Art is preserved in the divine power; it is bestowed upon whom He wills, and withdrawn. **And Morienes** <note>Morienus Romanus, a legendary hermit who taught the art to King Khalid</note>: It is fitting for you to know that the <term>mastery; the Great Work of alchemy</term> is nothing other than the secret and <term>arcanum; a hidden or mysterious secret</term> of the **Glorious God**.

The third reason is described by **Hermes** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of Hermeticism</note>: lest the wicked become powerful enough to commit sins. **And by Rosinus** <note>a Latinized name for Zosimos of Panopolis, a 3rd-century alchemist</note>: lest any evildoer, having obtained this stone, should perform illicit acts, which would lead to his own ruin.

The fourth is found in the same **Hermes**: namely, lest the Philosophers be compelled to give an account of those things which the wicked might do unjustly through their confidence in this art.

**Pythagoras** in the ***Turba*** <note>original: *Turba Philosophorum* or *The Assembly of the Philosophers*, one of the oldest Latin alchemical texts</note> provides the fifth: God has hidden this from the common people, lest the world be devastated. **And Alphidius** <note>An Arabic-Latin alchemical author, often cited in the 12th-14th centuries</note>: Some of the Philosophers, fearing God, did not hold this <term>arcanum; secret knowledge</term> to be so sublime and precious [in their own right], but rather wished to write their work openly; yet they were terrified to do so, because it would destroy the world, and the work of planting, bearing, and plowing would perish. Therefore, they asked God that He might deliver them from this world without punishment; God then taught them to compose a veiled book, and to write the treatises of the wise within it.

**Rhazes** <note>original: *Rhasis*; Abu Bakr al-Razi (c. 865–925), a Persian polymath and alchemist</note> gives the sixth: If, he says, I wished to explain all things exactly as they are, there would no longer be any place for prudence, since the foolish would be made equal to the wise,

# P A N D O R A ,

...when I read it again later, the following words were written in elegant letters:

> **Greetings, guest:** if perhaps you have heard anything of the King’s wedding, weigh these words carefully. Through us, the bridegroom offers you the choice of four paths. By any of these, provided you do not slip into detours, you may reach his Royal court. The first path is short but dangerous, and leads you among various rocks from which it will be difficult to extricate yourself. The second is longer; it leads you around but not away. It is level and easy, provided that with the help of the **Magnet** <note>original: "Magnetis"; likely referring to the "Magnet of the Sages" mentioned on the previous page, which guides the seeker</note> you do not allow yourself to be led away to the right or the left. The third is truly Royal, which will make the way pleasant for you through various delights and spectacles of our King. But this has happened to scarcely one in a thousand until now. By the fourth, it will be permitted to no man to reach the Royal court, seeing as it is consuming, and suitable only for **incorruptible bodies** <note>original: "corporibus incorruptibilibus"; a reference to the spiritualized or perfected state of matter</note>. Choose now from the [first] three which one you wish, and remain constant in it. But know that whichever you have entered, it is so destined for you by immutable **Fate**, and it is not lawful to turn back except at the greatest peril of your life.

> **These are the things** we wished you to know: but lo, take care not to ignore with how much danger you have committed yourself to this path. For if you know yourself to be guilty of even the smallest offense against the laws of our King: I beg you, while it is still permitted, return home as quickly as possible by the same way you came.

As soon as I had read this writing, all my joy vanished; and I, who had previously been singing happily, now began to weep inwardly. For I saw all three paths <note>original: "drey Weg"; although the inscription mentioned four, the fourth is deemed impossible for mortal men, leaving three viable options.</note> before me and knew that I was permitted, according to the time, to choose one for myself. I also saw the **fourth path** before me, but it was so surrounded by **fire and smoke** <note>original: "Feuer und Dampff"; in alchemy, this represents the "Way of Violence" or the "Dry Path" of high heat, which destroys those who are unprepared</note> that I did not dare go anywhere near it. There are several mad fools and blind men who say they can make **potable gold** <note>original: "Aurum potabile"; a legendary alchemical medicine consisting of gold in a liquid, drinkable form</note> or drinkable gold from or out of common gold; they also believe that it is excellent and the very best thing for healing all illnesses. This essence also **contains within itself that true medicinal Element of fire** <note>original: "quod & in se continet verum illud medicinale Elementum ignis"</note>, **conquering and penetrating all things** <note>original: "omnia vincens & penetrans"</note>. This is done so that the primordial **essences and virtues of the sun** <note>original: "essentiae & virtutes solis"; in alchemy, the sun is the celestial counterpart to gold</note> might manifest and give of themselves **with color and scent** <note>original: "cum colore & odore"</note> during the **Work** <note>original: "Operation"</note>. Once assured of this, the craftsman may proceed with good cheer **to the remaining steps** <note>original: "ad reliqua"</note> and faithfully apply himself to the philosophical **dissolution** <note>original: "solution"</note> in God’s name as a qualified **son of doctrine** <note>original: "Doctrinae filius"; a traditional term for a student initiated into the secret alchemical teachings</note>. With comforting assurance, his labor and expenses will be repaid a thousandfold, returning to him with every benefit.

## Saint Thomas Aquinas:

The matter of the Stone, however, is a coarse or thick water; the acting force is a heat or a cold that affects it. (d)

(d) <note>original: "Est ergo materia lapidis aqua grossa, agens autem est calor vel frigus congelans illam aquam & ad essentiam lapidis in actum deducens. Et credas virtuosiores lapides qui procedunt ab animalibus quam alios."</note> Therefore, the matter of the stone is a thick water, but the active agent is heat or cold, congealing that water and bringing it forth into the essence of the stone. And you should believe that those stones that proceed from animals <note>Alchemists often distinguished between mineral, vegetable, and animal sources for their materials; "animal" stones were often considered to possess a higher degree of "life" or spirit.</note> are more potent than others.

->Thomas Aquinas<-

And you should believe that these are the more precious stones—those which come forth from animals—than any others. Yet you can prepare no kind of stone without the thin greenness <note>German: *Grün dünnech*. This refers to *viriditas*, the "greenness" or vital life force alchemists believed existed even within metals, representing their capacity for growth and transformation.</note> and the "thinness" <note>In this context, "thin" likely refers to a volatile or spiritualized substance, as opposed to the "thick" or "coarse" matter of the physical world.</note> which belongs and grows in our mines or ore-veins. (a)

(a) <note>original: "Magister. Fili, scias, quod æs Philosophorum est aurum ipsorum. Unde Aristoteles ait, in libro suo: Aurum nostrum, non aurum vulgi: quia illa viriditas, quæ est in eo corpore, est tota perfectio ejus. Quia illa viriditas, per nostrum magisterium cito vertitur in aurum verissimum. Et de hoc..."</note> The Master says: Son, know that the copper of the Philosophers is their gold. # PANDORA,

<margin>(a)</margin>But through the long *decoction* <note>the process of heating or boiling a substance to extract its essence</note> and constant heat, it always becomes a little thicker in its rising and falling—*NB.* <note>Latin "Nota Bene," meaning "Note Well"</note> it *dissolves* and *coagulates* <note>turns from liquid to solid</note>—however, this does not happen so quickly. For the entire body must first be fully dissolved, rise up into the heights, and complete its course in its circle <note>referring to "circulation," where vapors rise, condense, and fall back down in a continuous cycle</note>. Therefore, do not let yourself be led astray if it does not happen soon, for Nature does not hurry, and yet it happens eventually; it also becomes browner. And should it be that something remains of the *Mercury* <note>original: "Mercurio"; the volatile or liquid principle in the work</note>, the process eventually consumes it so that it becomes *spiritual* <note>original: "spiritualisch"; meaning it has been refined into a vaporous or exalted state</note>. For the entire Art is thereafter nothing more than that the stone *dissolves* and *coagulates*; this occurs solely through *putrefaction* <note>the stage of "rotting" or breakdown, often associated with the color black, which must precede new growth</note>, through which it becomes *spiritual*.

Take then the thing which we are pleased to call **Gold**; yet it is not gold, and yet in truth it is Gold; it is metallic and yet comes from a mineral which Art—with the help of Nature—renews. ...sharp power of the poison of our <term>Mercury</term> <note>original: *Mercurii*; in alchemy, this is not just common quicksilver, but the "philosophical" solvent capable of breaking down metals.</note>, which brings everything it finds and which resists it into a pure dust—or rather into an inconceivable powder—and dissolves it. <meta>This page continues the commentary on the alchemical "gift of God" mentioned on the previous page, specifically explaining the metaphors used to describe the Philosopher's Stone (the venerable stone, the sublime mountain, and the open sea) and crediting the lineage of alchemical wisdom from Hermes Trismegistus to Paracelsus.</meta>

# Or the Noblest Gift of God.

The author frequently warns his disciples to recognize this unique gift of God with due reverence, and to drive away and exclude all fools and witless ones from it. Furthermore, he describes certain properties of the **stone** <term>lapis; referring to the Philosopher's Stone, the goal of the alchemical work</term>, calling it "hidden," which means known to few; "venerable," which means held in the highest esteem; and "splendid in color," which means the deepest red. For **redness** <term>rubedo; the final stage of the alchemical process, indicating success and perfection</term> is the most certain sign of final perfection. 

He speaks of a "sublime mind," <note>original: *mentem sublimem*; likely a play on words with "sublime mountain" (*montem sublimem*) from the previous page's imagery.</note> that is, a spirit **sublimated** <note>In alchemy, sublimation is the process where a solid is heated into a vapor and then condensed back into a solid, often used as a metaphor for spiritual purification.</note> and exalted. He mentions an "open sea," that is, the perpetual **mercurial water** <term>aqua mercurialis; the "living" solvent used to dissolve metals</term>, which is fixed and remains stable even in the fire. 

The stone contains all these properties within itself, which no one can know so precisely before its completion; but they finally burst forth when it stands prepared. This is no different than how one cannot know what kind of fruit a **pear tree** will push forth until you finally see clearly with your own eyes that it has produced pears—not apples, nor plums, nor cherries, nor fruits of any other kind. 

Therefore, because **Hermes** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure considered the "father" of alchemy.</note> knew all these powers and properties in the stone through his own experience, he also generously communicates them by teaching his disciples, who have not yet reached such experience, so that they might perceive some usefulness and benefit from this. However, he does not wish glory and praise to be given to himself for this faithful instruction, but to God. "Give thanks to God," he says, "who taught you this science." 

Hermes plants; **Paracelsus** <note>The famous 16th-century Swiss-German physician and alchemist who revolutionized the field.</note> waters; God <note>This is a paraphrase of 1 Corinthians 3:6: "I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth."</note>

<meta>catchword: au- (likely "auget" or "augat," meaning "gives the increase")</meta>

# PANDORA

**Patience**—and because it is necessary in our **Mastery**—haste is of the **Devil's part** in this Mastery. (a)

<gloss>(a) You researchers of this art cannot reach any useful result without a patient soul and a continuous regimen. Therefore, he who gladly practices **patience** <note>original Latin: *patientia*</note> should enter into this arrangement; but he who desires to arrive too quickly should not look into our books, because they cause great harm before they are understood by readers once, twice, or even three times.</gloss>

For whoever plants trees does not hope for fruit from them except after some time. And the sower does not hope to reap, except after the coming harvest. How then do you wish to have this result by reading a book only once, or by having experienced only the first part of the regimen? Therefore, do not be weary of proceeding and working toward the second and third parts of the regimen. Do this so that the **King crowned with the Red Diadem** <term>The "Red King" represents the Rubedo, the final stage of the Great Work where the philosopher's stone is perfected and the "gold" is produced.</term> appears.

->William of Texena<- <note>original: *Guilielmus Tecenensis*; a 14th-century alchemical author whose works often emphasized the slow, natural growth of the "Stone" like a plant.</note>

Although the time required will be longer, it matters little to you; prefer what is certain to what is uncertain. For by great heat you can destroy your work, but with a small fire, never.

<meta>This page continues the technical description of the alchemical process from page 292. # Or the Noblest Gift of God:

The water is joined with the earth in its smallest parts <note>original: *per minima*</note>, until the entire body becomes one.

It does not flow on the glass like other water when it is circulated; it possesses almost the nature of an oil, because it does not dissolve into water like another substance. For this reason, it is called an **oily vapor** <term>vapor unctuosus; a thick, fatty steam or moisture that alchemists believed contained the "soul" or life-force of the matter.</term>, which is very difficult to drive upward. For the water performs the **dissolving** <term>solution; the process of turning a solid into liquid, often the first step in the Great Work.</term>, the air the **rising** <term>Sublimation; the process where a substance is heated into vapor and then solidifies again, used here to represent spiritualization.</term>, the fire the **melting** <term>liquefaction; the state of becoming liquid through heat.</term>, and the **solidifying** <term>coagulation; the stage where the liquid "fixes" into a solid, stable form.</term> creates the earth. In this way, the four elements accomplish their work only through the medium of heat, and each one hastens toward the completion of its own creation. Thus, the body is broken by its own self, as has been said. It dissolves itself, sublimes itself, kills itself, and brings itself back to life. This action occurs without ceasing. 

That is <note>original: *Id est*</note>, in our Water <note>original: *Aqua nostra*; the "Philosophical Water" or "mercury of the wise," which is the primary solvent in the work.</note> all methods occur: namely sublimation, distillation, solution, calcination, and fixation. Therefore, our grinding <note>original: *contritio*</note> is not done by hands, but by the strongest boiling <note>original: *decoctione*; an intense, prolonged heating process.</note>. What I have said is true, for this entire **Great Work** <term>magisterium; the mastery or completion of the alchemical process, often used to refer to the creation of the Philosopher's Stone.</term> consists of one thing and one single path.

Nature performs all of this alone through the medium of her heat, which drives the natural elements forward and separates them during their transformation. They do not truly part from one another; rather, the separation is nothing more than a change from one state into the other: From the water, air is created...

# P A N D O R A,

...out of the air, fire; and out of the fire, in turn, earth.

**Aristotle:** When you have obtained water from air, air from fire, and fire from earth, then you will possess the complete Art <note>original: *plenam artem*. While Aristotle was the foundational philosopher for the four elements, alchemists often attributed specific "recipes" for the Stone to him. Bernard of Trevisan, a 15th-century alchemist, discusses this specific elemental argument in his second book.</note>.

For the elements are not separated in the way that fools imagine; rather, it is called a "separation" for the sake of describing the transformation. Nature herself joins them back together again without discord. Thus, within this body, the spirit and the soul are separated during the transformation, yet they also reunite themselves; for the soul rests in the spirit as if in its own seat and proper place where it belongs.

For the Philosophers have said that our **Stone** <term>Lapis; the Philosophers' Stone, the goal of the Great Work, representing a perfect balance of spirit and matter.</term> is composed of Body, Soul, and Spirit <note>original: *Corpore, Anima & Spiritu*</note>, and they speak the truth.

The moisture of the spirit is entirely water—**only a single Water throughout** <note>original: *Unica tantum Aqua per totum*</note>—and the moisture of the soul is entirely oil; our Stone is an **oily vapor** <note>original: *vapor unctuosus*</note>. For the soul is a bond for the spirit, just as the body is a bond for the soul; such a link is nothing but a bond of nature.

Our entire operation is nothing other than the extraction of water from the earth, and the pouring of this water back over the earth until the earth **putrefies** <term>putrefactio; the "black stage" of the process where the material breaks down. Alchemists saw this as a necessary death that precedes spiritual rebirth.</term>. For this earth rots along with the water and is puri- <note>The text breaks here; the catchword indicates the word continues on the next page as *mundificatur*, meaning "purified."</note>

# OR THE NOBLEST GIFT OF GOD.

[...as children] grow, they do not eat and drink much; but the larger they grow, the more they eat and drink. So it is also in our mastery regarding the soaking of the water. Therefore, you should rub the **earth** <term>earth: original Latin *terram*, referring to the solid base material or "body" of the alchemical work</term> with great seriousness and diligence, and **imbibe** it <term>imbibe: from the Latin *imbibere*, meaning to saturate or "feed" a dry solid with a liquid until it is absorbed</term> from one eight-day period to the next with the cooking and gentle **calcination** <term>calcination: the process of heating a substance to a high temperature to reduce it to a dry, friable powder</term>. Do not let yourself be vexed by performing the work often—the **coagulation** <term>coagulation: the thickening or solidifying of a liquid into a mass</term>, the grinding, and the imbibing of the water—for without this labor, your earth brings forth no fruit. Through this work, the water becomes one with the earth.

But you should not withdraw your hand from the grinding, the imbibing, and the **roastings** <note>original: *Bratungen*; the text uses culinary metaphors to describe the gentle application of heat</note> or coagulation, until the water becomes completely dry and has been "drunk" and swallowed by the white earth. For this drinking and coagulation, combined with constant **attrition** <term>attrition: original Latin *contrition*, the intensive grinding or wearing down of a substance into the finest possible powder</term> and roasting, are what make the earth white. 

Yet, take care that you do not imbibe the earth except with great seriousness and a long period of grinding after the soaking. You should always note the weight, so that the great **tincture** <term>tincture: the potent, concentrated essence produced at the end of the Work, capable of transforming or "coloring" other substances</term> or the remaining moisture does not spoil the work during its preparation. As long as you cook the matter with roasting, that much moisture shall [serve] to **dissolve** <term>dissolve: original Latin *dissolviren*, the process of turning a solid back into a liquid state</term>...

# OR GOD'S NOBLEST GIFT. <note>original: "Oder Edelst Gab Gottes."</note>

Just as winter is deprived of all fruit and natural acting power, so too this work of **contrition** <term>Contrition: In alchemy, the "contritionum" refers to the physical grinding or pulverizing of materials into a fine powder, the first stage of breaking down substances.</term> still seems to be, and is, deprived of every active operation of the elixir, because nothing of the aforementioned substances has yet been mixed. Thus it is clear that one always begins in winter; any time is the "winter" of the elixir, and the work can be performed. When the time of winter is completed and finished with the crushing of those mentioned species, the work of composition and the mixing of said species by the hands of the **Artificer** <note>original: "Artificis." The alchemist was often called the Artist or Artificer, signifying someone who assists nature through skill.</note> begins immediately. This is called the work of **spring**, because just as natural things are naturally united in spring to bear fruit, so every single thing from which the elixir is generated or composed in this work is united to bear fruit or to generate the **Philosopher’s Stone** <note>original: "lapidem philosophicum."</note>. And so it is clear that the work of spring in the elixir begins immediately when winter is finished, and it can be done at any time.

Next follows **summer**, which occurs when the "water" ascends from those species, just as the sap of trees and plants <note>original: "planetarum." While the text says "planets," in this context it likely refers to the "planets" or metals of the laboratory, or is a common scribal error for "plantarum" (plants).</note> rises within them and makes them flourish, and just as plants and herbs produce flowers in summer. The alembic is the lid of the still; its changing color signals a successful chemical reaction.</note> at the end of the composition of the often-mentioned water. This composition or completion of the water is called summer.

Then, immediately, the other species are dissolved—namely the **white ferment** and **red ferment**, the **red earth**, and **Mercury**—within that same water. And here begins the fourth season of the year, which is called **autumn**,

...once it has been conceived, **Saturn** <note>The alchemical name for lead.</note> can never be brought into the state of such [noble] metals by the **Archeus** <term>Archeus</term> <note>original: "Archæo"; in the philosophy of Paracelsus, this is the "inner artisan" or vital force of nature that directs the growth of minerals and living things.</note>. It is fair to ask how this can be, since the mine at **Villach** is just as old as the one in the **Harz**, and **Villach** is located in a warmer region than **Goslar** and **Zellerfeld** <note>Mining towns in the Harz region.</note>; what then prevents the "good Saturn" from rising to a higher degree of perfection?

Many will conclude and say: it is the fault of the seed, or to be blamed on impure accidents. They thereby treat the **generation of metals** <note>original: "Generationem metallorum"</note> as if they were all made from the same mold, claiming that whatever **Mars** <term>Mars</term> <note>The alchemical name for iron.</note> and **Venus** <term>Venus</term> <note>The alchemical name for copper.</note> are made of, gold also comes from that same source and is identical in its **root** <note>original: "radice"</note>. Therefore, they believe that if such lesser metals were purified and **digested** <note>The process of exposing a substance to gentle, continuous heat to mature it.</note>, they could become good **gold**.

But they are missing the mark by a wide margin <note>literally "missing by a large peasant's shoe."</note>. A hare is no cow, even if it has four legs and occasionally gives milk. The lesser metals do not possess enough power and perfection for the **Universal Tincture** <term>Universal Tincture</term> <note>original: "Universal-Tinctur"; the legendary "Philosopher's Stone" in liquid form, capable of transmuting base metals and curing all illness.</note> to be made from them alone, although it cannot be denied that the "seed" is within them (albeit in a very small quantity).

For the **Philosophical Soul** <note>original: "Philosophische Anima"; the vital, volatile essence of the matter being worked upon.</note> is something far different than, say, **White Lead** <note>original: "Bleyweiß"; basic lead carbonate, a common pigment.</note>; its **Gum** is something much different than **Sugar of Lead** <note>original: "Sacharum Saturni"; lead acetate, a sweet-tasting but toxic salt.</note>; its **Butter and Oil** or **Gur** <term>Gur</term> <note>A term used by miners and alchemists for a "primordial juice" or gelatinous mineral state found in the earth, believed to be the raw material from which metals grow.</note> is, compared to that from common lead, as different as day is from night.

In considering this explanation, let the beginning students beware of **common Saturn** <note>Ordinary metallic lead.</note>; though he is indeed the signpost to the **noble virgin’s womb** <note>An allegorical term for the pure, receptive state of matter required for the Great Work.</note>, he is not for that reason the noble virgin herself. For the sake of honor, I must confess of **Saturn** that, next to **God**, he led me to the knowledge of his **dear cousins** <note>original: "Basen"; likely referring to the other metallic spirits or the related "Philosophical" substances.</note>. May God grant grace that everyone after me may find the straight-as-a-string path and come out of the darkness into the light.

->Heinrich von Battsdorff.<- <note>The pseudonym of Heinrich von Batsdorff, likely Christian Reibi, a 17th-century alchemical writer.</note>

<meta>This page follows from page 433, which concluded with a warning that many fail to understand the alchemical Art because they lack either divine favor or the willingness to apply their reason. # P A N D O R A,

<margin>(p)</margin>
<margin><unclear>mark</unclear></margin>

The entire work of the <term>magisterium|The "mastery" or Great Work of alchemy, representing the full process of creating the Philosopher's Stone.</term> of the great and hidden **Philosopher's Stone** consists of two parts of operation. The first part concerns the operations of the **elixir**, and is called the "first work." The second part concerns the operation of the **stone**, and is called the "second work," which is performed differently and in a different vessel. Once the first operation of the elixir is completed, the other begins—which is the second—concerning the operation of the stone. 

Some philosophers in their books first handed down the second work—namely, the operation of the stone—and afterwards the first work, which concerns the elixir. And some speak now of one work, now of the other, knowingly entangling themselves and pursuing their intention obscurely, and explaining it even more obscurely. They did this so that they might deceive <note>original: "fatuos," meaning foolish or superficial seekers.</note> foolish seekers and those possessing a hard or coarse wit, and so that they might thoroughly hide this deservedly famous science, while simultaneously enticing the prudent toward it and manifesting it to them. 

We, however, will maintain the right order in this operation of the stone, just as we have proven with our own fingers, and touched, and seen with our eyes, in this book. For it is necessary first that things be "elixated"—that is, converted into an **elixir**—before one intends the operation of the stone; otherwise, no one will in any way reach the discovery and operation of the great and true stone. # Or the Noblest Gift of God.

In Kuttenberg <note>Kutná Hora, a famous silver and copper mining town in the Kingdom of Bohemia (modern-day Czech Republic).</note> they smelt Marcasite <note>A common iron sulfide mineral, often confused with pyrite.</note>, and make copper out of iron; which is not only better in quality, but also allows itself to be hammered more easily. To treat this at greater length is not my intention, because two or three examples are enough to confirm the truth. I must proceed further to the making of gold, and prove that such is much more possible; and conclude that what is possible in higher and greater things can happen much more so and sooner in lesser and more closely related ones. For nature, through its cooking and purification, makes gold and silver from sulfur and mercury, which artists imitate, desiring to make their gold and silver from the Mercury <term>Mercury|☿</term>, Sun <term>Gold|☉</term>, and Jupiter <term>Tin|♃</term> of the Philosophers <note>original: *Philosophorum*. This refers to the "sophic" or alchemical versions of these elements, rather than common metals.</note>.

If there is now one single determined Matter in nature, which is simple and plain, then one must not fall from one thing to another in the Art, making mixtures, performing contrary operations <note>original: *operationes*</note>, and using marvelous furnaces, of which the books of the alchemists are full. It would be no wonder if every soot-burner <note>original: *Unckenbrenner*. A derogatory term for a "puffer" or a bumbling, unrefined alchemist who labors at the furnace without understanding the underlying theory.</note> had attained the truth of this Art through unceasing labor and diligence, if nothing more were required than mere knowledge.

# P A N D O R A ,

[nothing among] perishable things is more to be desired than this art, by which the separation of natural bodies from their binary state <term>binario: a state of duality or opposition, often representing the separation of spirit and matter</term> is taught, along with their bringing into union through a ternary <term>ternarium: a triad or state of three-in-one, representing the reconciliation and perfection of the substance</term>. Indeed, no better model could be given for the human resurrection than from this teaching. For the author suggests that the natural bodies of inanimate things, once divided from their spirits and purged, can be joined to them again for resurrection—that is, for perfection. Just as human bodies are separated from their spirits or souls by death, so that later, by the will of God alone, they may rise again into eternal life through a union better than the first. In exactly the same way, [the author] teaches that through the artificial corruption of inanimate bodies (which is called Chemical death <note>original: "mors Chemistica"</note>), one may separate their spirits and souls, leading to the reduction of their ternary state into unity; that is, to a better life—not an eternal one, certainly, but one more excellent than that which they previously held by nature. For inanimate things live within themselves by a hidden motion <note>original: "occulto motu"; the alchemical belief that all matter possesses an internal vitality</note>, and after they have reached union, they most clearly reveal this life through their operations upon other bodies, so that they make those also live without their own corruption, until the final end of their incorrupt nature has arrived.

# THE NOBLEST GIFT OF GOD.

[at the] beginning, it tinctures <term>tingirt: to dye or transform the substance of a base metal into a noble one.</term> 10 parts; and if it is multiplied once, it tinctures 100 parts; the second time, 1000 parts; and so forth. Because of this, it is called a treasure that lacks nothing, a Stone that impregnates itself and gives birth to itself, and as the proverb says: the *Cornu copiae* <note>Latin: "Horn of Plenty."</note>. With silver, the same work can be undertaken, with the only difference being that for silver, one does not need any antimony or cement <term>Cement: a dry refining mixture used to purify precious metals by removing impurities through heat.</term> to refine it at the beginning. Instead, one drives the silver one, two, or three times from the cupel <term>Cappellen: a porous vessel used in assaying to separate precious metals from base metals like lead.</term> to the highest degree of purity, makes it fine, and beats it into a round plate. The colors will also return; otherwise, the process occurs in all things with the one as with the other. Of these multiplications, there is not just one way, but many, and they are performed according to the reason and experience of the artist <term>Künſtler: the alchemist or practitioner of the Hermetic art.</term>. While one practitioner may bring it to a red powder and another into a brittle mass, this is of no importance, provided the work itself is correct.

# P A N D O R A ,

...for if water extracted from ashes <note>original: "aqua extracta à cineribus" — this refers to lye, a primary ingredient in historical soap-making.</note> and oil are taken with certain other things, and boiled with a specific **decoction** <term>Decoction: The process of boiling a substance, usually in water, to extract its essence or chemical properties.</term>, soap is generated from them. But if each ingredient were taken by itself and boiled until it solidified, and afterwards someone tried to compose soap from them, he would not be able to do so. 

**Sulfur**, however, was in the beginning water, its nature cold and moist; and afterwards it was converted into air, the nature of which is hot and moist; then indeed into fire, the nature of which is hot and dry. Later, the water tempered itself with that same fire, and it was the composition of **male and female** <note>This refers to the "Alchemical Marriage," the union of active/male and passive/female principles to create a balanced substance.</note>. 

And we say, therefore, that even if it is granted that the nature, or root, of minerals is **quicksilver** <note>original: "argentum vivum" — Mercury.</note> with sulfur, we nevertheless ought not to take the raw elements from which mineral bodies are formed, but rather we ought to take that which is derived from those mineral bodies themselves. A clear example of this is found in plants. 

For we know that the generation of a plant comes from water combined with a subtle earthy substance, as we said before; and yet if we were to take [raw] water and earth, we would never generate a plant. We do not, therefore, take the raw materials from which the plant is made, but rather the thing from which the living organism comes, which is derived from the plant—namely, its **egg** <note>original: "ovum" — used here to mean a seed or the concentrated "germ" of a plant.</note>. Once we know that this egg is generated from subtle earth mixed with that water, we entrust it to the earth until that which was incomplete is made whole.

# Or the Noblest Gift of God.

By its heat, the sun warms the earth, and a part of that heat remains in the interior of the earth; and when the sun has risen above the earth and finds that heat is hidden within the earth, it is naturally necessary for heat like itself to ascend, together with a part of the newly generated heat. When it encounters any part of water, it dissolves it and converts it into vapor. This vapor indeed moves upward until a proportionate heat <note>original: "calor proportionabilis" — a balanced level of heat necessary for alchemical transformation.</note> flows over it; but when the sun descends toward the west, the proportionate heat is diminished until the vapor is condensed and descends by distilling.

(b) Metallic principles differ in a threefold state: they are either the **most remote**, such as a mixture of earth with water; or **remote**, like vitriol <note>original: *vitriolum*. ## Or the Noblest Gift of God.

Sulfur has within it two causes of breaking or destruction: a pure flammable substance, and an earthly dross <note>original: "Trusigkeit" — referring to impurities or dregs found in raw minerals.</note>. For through the first, it does not persist, nor does it allow persistence <note>In alchemy, "standing" or "persisting" refers to "fixity"—the ability of a substance to remain stable under the heat of fire without evaporating.</note>; for it always burns and is burned, and it creates blackness in every work. Through the other cause, however, it has neither fluidity nor entry; for if it is fixed or attached, it prevents pouring, and it can never be attached unless it is first calcined <term>calciniert: the process of heating a substance to high temperatures to drive off volatile parts or reduce it to a powder (calx)</term>. But if it is calcined, it cannot be cast by any art <note>original: "Kunst" — a common term for the "Art" of Alchemy.</note>, for it is entirely reduced to an earthly substance. (1)

(1) <note>original Latin: "Potest ergo sulphur cum sit proprium coagulamentum argenti vivi..."</note> Therefore, sulfur—since it is the proper coagulant of quicksilver <term>argentum vivum: mercury</term>—can be of various colors, and can be fixed <note>Resistant to fire.</note> or volatile, in small, large, or equal amounts. But quicksilver, as it is always white—and whiteness is like the elemental basis of colors in which all colors may vary—therefore quicksilver receives the diversities of all colors from sulfur. Because of this, every metal is colored with a different color, and other various substances are generated, such as Marcasite <note>A term often used for iron pyrites or other metallic sulfides.</note>, Magnesia <note>In this period, often referring to manganese ore or other dark mineral additives.</note>, Antimony, and Tutia <term>Thutia: zinc oxide, often collected as a crust from the flues of smelting furnaces</term>.

Iron would also melt by virtue of the fixed quicksilver it contains, but the fixed sulfur in it greatly overpowers and hinders it. On the other hand, non-fixed sulfur is the cause of softness, volatility in fire, and melting without glowing, as in Saturn and Jupiter. For both of these bodies are only "half-digested" <note>semidigesta: an alchemical concept where "lesser" metals were thought to be "unripe" or not fully matured by nature's heat</note> and, through solidification, are only slightly removed from the nature of quicksilver. From this it is clear that whichever bodies melt slowly, solidify quickly, and vice versa.

For it arises only in these **bodies** <note>original German: *Cörpern*; referring to the metallic substances</note> / and therefore we prepare these bodies to be subtle and pure. (i)

<gloss>(i) Bodies differ in their composition from **quicksilver** <note>original: *argento vivo*</note>, from which they are generated: in the same manner that the mercury itself was pure or impure, or derived from clean or unclean sulfur.</gloss>

If quicksilver is coagulated from pure sulfur, in which there is a simple fiery power, it will be **gold** <note>original: *aurum*</note>.

If the sulfur is weak, and the **Mercury** <note>original: *Mercurius*</note> is of good substance, it converts it into **copper** <note>original: *æs*; in alchemical Latin, this can refer to copper, bronze, or brass.</note>.

But if the quicksilver is heavy, earthy, and unclean, and the sulfur is unclean, foul-smelling, and earthy, and of a fixed substance, **iron** <note>original: *ferrum*</note> is made therefrom.

Thus metallic bodies differ from quicksilver according to the amount of foreign or burning sulfur present within them.

A large quantity of sulfur is their imperfection, and a large quantity of Mercury is their perfection.

Sulfur burns and is burned, and it hinders perfection in every alchemical work.

Sulfur is twofold, namely **living** <note>original: *vivum*; often meaning native or philosophic sulfur</note> and **burning** <note>original: *urens*; common sulfur which causes impurities</note>.

The more simple the sulfur is, the more it delights in and clings to simple and clean **Mercury** <note>original Latin: *Mercurio*</note>.

Common sulfur <note>original Latin: *Sulphur vulgi*; referring to ordinary, brimstone sulfur which was considered too "foul" for the work.</note> always infects and blackens; it corrupts in whatever manner it is prepared by art; therefore it is not the sulfur of the philosophers.

# Or the Noblest Gift of God.

...thus the perfect **body** <note>original: *Corpus*</note> helps the imperfect one, and completes it, and makes it perfect, without the admixture of any other external thing. (k)

<margin>(k) Now to the point: namely, that these **three beginnings** <note>In the alchemical tradition of Paracelsus, these are Salt, Sulfur, and Mercury, known as the *Tria Prima*.</note> are entirely and absolutely necessary, because they are the **immediate matter** <note>original: *nechste Materi*</note>. For the matter of metals is of two kinds: a near one and a distant one. The near one is **sulfur and quicksilver** <term>Sulfur and Mercury: the two primary principles believed to compose all metals.</term>; the distant ones are the four elements, from which God alone can create anything.</margin>

Therefore, abandon the elements, for you cannot and are not able to make anything out of them except these three beginnings; considering that nature itself brings forth nothing else from them. If you then can bring nothing other than these three beginnings out of the elements, what purpose does this vain labor serve you, to seek or make that which is already created by nature? Is it not better to walk three miles instead of four? Be content, therefore, that you have these three beginnings, from which nature makes all things on earth and under the earth, and which you can also find perfectly in all things. From this proper **separation and composition** <note>original: *Scheidung und Zusammensetzung*; these are the two fundamental actions of the alchemist, often referred to as *Spagyrics*.</note>...

<summary>This page advises the alchemist to work with the "three beginnings" (Salt, Sulfur, and Mercury) rather than the four elements, arguing that nature has already performed the difficult task of transforming elements into these intermediate principles. It defines these as the "near matter" of metals, essential for the alchemical process.</summary>

### PANDORA;

...nature works <note>original: *[berie]tet*; likely continuing from 'prepares' or 'arranges' on the previous page</note> in stones as well as metals in the mineral kingdom; in the vegetable kingdom, however, in trees, herbs, and everything: and in animals also **body** <note>original: *Leib* or *Corpus*</note>, **spirit** <note>original: *Geist*</note>, and **soul** <note>original: *Seel*</note>, which is primarily compared to the **Philosophical Work** <term>Philosophical Work: Also known as the *Magnum Opus* or Great Work, the process of creating the Philosopher's Stone.</term>. The **body** <note>original: *Corpus*</note> is the earth; the **spirit** is the water; and the **soul** is the fire or the **sulfur of gold** <term>Sulfur of Gold: The active, solar principle believed to give gold its permanence and red color.</term>. The spirit increases the size of the body, but the fire increases its power. However, because there is more of the spirit by weight than of the fire, the spirit is raised up and suppresses the fire, drawing it into itself; and thus each of them grows in power, while the earth, which is between the two, grows in weight and heaviness.

->**Michael Sendivogius.**<-
<note>Sendivogius (1566–1636) was a famous Polish alchemist and chemist known for his theories on the "food of life" in the air (oxygen).</note>

The reason is that, in whatever way a body is prepared, it cannot acquire <term>fluidity</term> <note>original: "fluxibilitatem"; the ability of a substance to flow and penetrate other metals during the chemical "projection."</note> by its own power alone; nor can the spirit, in whatever way it is prepared, be changed from its nature or perfectly <term>fixed</term> <note>original: "figi"; the alchemical process of making a volatile substance stable and resistant to heat.</note> without the mediation of the body. It is necessary for the medicine to be fluid, living, capable of tinging, and permanent—which cannot happen at all without the tempering of the elements.

And without doubt, that tempering of the elements never seems to occur without the <term>conjunction</term> <note>original: "conjunctione"; the chemical and symbolic union of opposites, such as "body" and "spirit" or "male" and "female."</note> of body and spirit, because through their union the deficiency of the elements is supplied, both on the part of the body and on the part of the spirit; thus the body is made spiritual, and the spirit is made corporeal.

# PANDORA,

...be deprived of moisture, the body to be **calcined** <note>original Latin: "calcinandum"</note>, but only so that its structural continuity is broken and it is reduced to the smallest possible particles. Just as there is a great variety of substances to be calcined, so too are there various reasons for calcination. Indeed, the **Philosophical Earth** <term>Philosophical Earth: The "base" or "soil" of the alchemical work, often referring to the solid matter remaining after initial purifications</term> is calcined so that it may be freed from all "oiliness" <note>Refers to combustible impurities or sulfurous residues</note>, and that it may become open and spongy, allowing the "water" <note>An alchemical solvent or mercury</note> to enter more easily and perform its work. As **Raymond Lull** <note>Ramon Llull (c. 1232 – 1315), a Majorcan philosopher and mystic whose name was frequently attached to alchemical texts</note> says, it is done so that the matter can expand and grow, and within itself be suffocated, turned over, cleansed, purified, and converted into its own nature. Both imperfect and perfect metallic bodies are calcined. Likewise, spirits and other substances foreign to their nature—such as salts, vitriols <note>original Latin: "atramenta"; literally "blacking," but used in alchemy to refer to dark sulfates/vitriols</note>, and alums—are also calcined.

The second is that one should dissolve the spirits and strengthen the metals. The third is that one dissolves the metals and strengthens the spirits. The fourth is the best counsel: that one dissolves the metals with the spirits. (c)

### Or the Noblest Gift of God.

...coagulates. In the previous chapter just before this, we touched upon and spoke as if in passing about what pertains somewhat to this matter. There we said that the **body** <term>Body: The solid, material part of a substance, often a metal, that undergoes transformation</term> which is dissolved is changed into a watery form: here let us say that the body which was denser before solution becomes thinner after solution through the **spirit** <term>Spirit: The volatile, "living" essence or vapor in alchemy, often associated with Mercury</term>, that is, the water. And conversely: The spirit which was thin and rare before the body’s solution becomes denser and thicker after the body’s solution. Therefore, through solution, the thick body becomes thin. Conversely, the thin spirit becomes thick.

So that this teaching might be better known, it was not troublesome to repeat the words of **Villanovanus** <note>Arnaldus de Villa Nova (c. 1240–1311), a celebrated Catalan physician and alchemist</note> himself in the same way, with the words somewhat changed but the sense not dissimilar, when he writes: **As much as the body is dissolved, so much is the spirit coagulated.** Because if the body were not dissolved, neither would the spirit be thickened. The same author says elsewhere, though a little more obscurely: That which comes out from the dissolved body is a **radiant humidity** <note>original Latin: "humiditas radiosa"</note> (which I therefore interpret as a **fertile tincture** <note>original Latin: "tincturam fœcundam"; a "tincture" is the concentrated essence used to transform or color metals</note>). That which dissolves the body comes forth from the spirit: its power is **germinal** <note>original Latin: "virtus germinosa"</note>, that is (for so I am pleased to explain it), filled with the power of multiplying.

While the body and spirit mutually enter into one another, there is such a great necessity and union between the two that one can no longer be separated from the other. Therefore, when Villanovanus had said: The **solution of the body** happens with the **coagulation of the spirit**, and the **coagulation of the spirit** with the **solution of the body**, he adds: Then the body is mixed with the spirit and becomes one with it; nor are they ever separated, any more than...

<summary>This page explains the reciprocal relationship in alchemy where the solid body dissolves into a liquid state while the volatile spirit solidifies, ultimately forming an inseparable union. Citing Arnaldus de Villa Nova, the author emphasizes that the "radiant humidity" released from this process possesses the power to multiply or "germinate" the alchemical work.</summary>

But indeed, regarding what I said—that in the dissolution the **body** and **spirit** <term>Body and Spirit: In alchemy, the "body" is the solid, material substance (often a metal), while the "spirit" is the volatile, active principle</term> mutually enter into one another—I would not want anyone to think that this union and interpenetration happens with any gap in time. You can read this very thing expressed nowhere more clearly than in the **Rosary of the Philosophers** <note>original: *Rosarium Philosophorum*, a major alchemical compendium</note>, where it is written thus from the first chapter of **Calid** <note>Khalid ibn Yazid (d. 704), a legendary early figure in Arabic and Latin alchemy</note>:

For the spirit is not coagulated except with the dissolution of the body, nor is the body dissolved except with the coagulation of the spirit. Therefore, there is no difference between the dissolution of the body and the coagulation, nor is there any diverse work in anything, such that one happens without the other. Just as we see happen when common water attempts to make earth more subtle and dissolve it into its own nature: at the same time, the water becomes denser and thicker, while the earth becomes more subtle and rarer.

## Or the Noblest Gift of God. <note>original: "Oder Edelst Gab Gottes"</note>

The joining together of the four elements; and it is called "one thing" when the substance of the metal and the substance of the water are prepared to be inseparable, so that one may not be separated from the other. Thus, one is a spirit—that is, **volatile** <note>original: "Volatilis"; a substance that evaporates or changes easily when heated</note>—and the other is **fixed** <note>original: "fix"; a substance that remains stable and does not evaporate under heat</note>; and conversely in the end, when one is **fixed**, let the other also be as the **body** <note>original: "Corpus"</note>.

<margin>(c)</margin> There are four principal regimes <note>stages of treatment or "government" of the chemical process</note> of our stone: namely, dissolving, washing, joining, and fixing. To dissolve <note>original: "solvere"</note> is to divide the bodies and create the raw matter. To wash <note>original: "abluere"</note> is to bury <note>original: "inhumare"; often referring to placing the vessel in a warm environment like a "bath" of sand or horse dung</note>, to distill, to ascend, and to descend. To join <note>original: "conjungere"</note> is to impregnate, to whiten, and to redden. To fix <note>original: "figere"</note>, indeed, is to ferment and to marry <note>original: "desponsare"; the symbolic union of substances</note>. Dissolving converts the Stone into its first nature, which is its water. Washing converts it into air. Joining converts it into fire. Fixing converts it into spiritual and dyeing <note>original: "tingentem"; possessing the power to change the color and quality of other metals</note> earth.

->*The Ladder of the Philosophers*<- <note>original: "Scala Philosophorum"; a title of a famous 14th-century alchemical treatise</note>

<margin>(cc)</margin> **Dissolution** <note>original: "solutio"</note> is fivefold: namely, the main dissolution; the dissolution of the elements; the philosophical dissolution; the dissolution of the ferment; and the dissolution of the Stone and **Elixir**.
