# P A N D O R A,
### Or the Most Noble Gift of God.

<margin>700</margin>
When the spirit of the **Sun** <note>original: "solis"; the alchemical name for gold</note> itself is impressed upon it, it passes into a solar state; if of the **Moon** <note>original: "Lunae"; the alchemical name for silver</note>, into a lunar state; thus it takes on the nature of the rest, whose metallic spirit it embraces. Therefore, in relation to its body, it is compared to those other mentioned spirits just as a wife is to her husband—not by a physical mixture, but when the spirit has been drawn out from the metal itself and cast into the **Mercury** <note>original: "Mercurium"</note> after preparation, only then does it manifest its **transmutation** <term>transmutatio: the alchemical transformation of one substance into another, typically base metals into gold</term>.

In the same way, the dead ore of metal is like an uncultivated field or earth; if it is softened or brought to life by the **philosophical plow** <note>a metaphorical tool or process in alchemy used to "break up" or prepare the material for transformation</note> (which remains fixed and incorruptible as the "female" in this work), it is united by the mentioned bodily spirit through degrees of fire into that nature and substance. And this occurs with the dead body of the metal, which certainly cannot happen with the crude spirit of Mercury. 

And even if the body of the Sun is Mercury or **quicksilver** <note>original: "argentum vivum"</note> and is fixed, common Mercury—being neither fixed nor yet "mortified" <note>in alchemy, "mortification" refers to the symbolic death or chemical breakdown of a substance before it can be purified</note>—likewise has not yet "risen." For the **resurrection of metals** <term>resurrectio metallorum: a stage where the "dead" chemical matter is reborn into a more perfect, spiritualized state</term> is an undying regeneration, and the means by which such **tinctures** <note>alchemical substances capable of changing the color and quality of metals</note> are advanced toward their own generation.

Therefore, it cannot be united with dead bodies to achieve fixation, but only with extracted spirits (acting as the aforementioned "bodies"), which are subject to metals just as common Mercury is subject to all metallic spirits. For the crude spirit of Mercury by no means generates this tincture in substance, any more than a concubine produces legitimate offspring.

->Gerardus Dorneus<-
<note>Gerard Dorn (c. 1530–1584) was a prominent philosopher and alchemist known for his detailed commentaries on Paracelsus and his focus on the spiritual and psychological aspects of alchemy.</note>

## Geber.

Geber <note>Jabir ibn Hayyan (c. 721–815), a foundational figure in alchemy whose Latinized name, Geber, was synonymous with alchemical authority in the Renaissance.</note> says: the hidden spirit is in the belly of its **body** <note>original: "corporis"</note>; this same spirit is our water, and our **quicksilver** <note>original: "Argentum Vivum"</note>, and our fire. It is called our fire because the spirit draws the hidden spirit to itself, and the oil draws the hidden **oil** <note>original: "oleum"</note> to itself. Thus, the water is a strong and true spirit; it draws the secret spirit from the body. You should add a little of this body into the mixture, and it will become a "water of the matter" <note>original: "Wasser materiæ"</note>. This water is extremely useful in the **Art** <term>the Art: a traditional shorthand for alchemy, specifically the "Great Work" of transmutation</term>, although it is not yet entirely perfect. This is because it is extracted from "small money" <note>likely referring to common or base metals of low value, as opposed to gold or silver</note>, and it is sharp and hard. Its bitterness is not yet certain, but it brings about a **restoration** <term>Widermachung: a term meaning restoration, restitution, or the act of making something whole again</term> of the unstable things from which it was extracted. For this reason, the **matter** <note>original: "Materia"</note> is called the "Necessity" <note>original: "Nothdurfft"; implying either a state of deprivation or the essential requirement for the process</note>. Through the fire, the matter dissolves, and that fire destroys and kills...

(f) Nature, in creating and forming metals, possesses a certain substance or matter—namely, **quicksilver** <note>original: "argentum vivum"; mercury</note> and **sulfur**, as has been said. Thus, Nature makes a spirit out of a body, and in this way makes it ascend from earth to heaven—that is, she makes a corporeal thing spiritual. And because Nature afterwards converts this spiritual matter into metal, as has been said, she then makes a body out of the spirit; and thus she makes it descend from heaven to earth—that is, she makes a spiritual thing corporeal in her operations and actions. In all these operations, however, we cannot truly follow Nature in a literal sense, but we are bound to follow her through as much similarity as possible in our work—

<page-num>617</page-num>
<page-type>text</page-type>
<header>Or the Noblest Gift of God.</header>

...make the volatile fixed again, so that it no longer rises during the process of sublimation <note>the transition of a substance from a solid to a gas and back to a solid</note>, but remains steadily at the bottom of the glass, and no longer flies away even in the fire <note>original: symbol $\nabla$ which usually denotes water, but here placed next to the word for fire</note>.

To dissolve <term>Solvere</term> <note>original: *Solvere*</note> is to divide, corrupt, or break the body <term>corpus</term> in order to make from it the prime matter <term>primam materiam</term> <note>the original, undifferentiated substance from which all things are created</note>: that is, that you dissolve the body into a water <note>original: symbol $\nabla$</note>.

To wash away <term>Abluere</term> <note>original: *Abluere*</note> or to wash off, is to make moist, to distill, and to calcine <note>to heat a substance until it turns to powder</note>.

To restore <term>Reducere</term> <note>original: *Reducere*</note> is when you give back to a dry body its water and its evaporated elements to drink once again.

To fix <term>Figere</term> <note>original: *Figere*</note> or to make stable, is when you again dissolve and coagulate that which is now joined together, using the first work: namely, through dissolving, nature is turned inward, specifically into water <note>original: symbol $\nabla$</note>; with the second work of our art, nature is turned outward; with the third, nature is turned again, namely when you sublime our Stone <note>the Philosopher's Stone, the goal of the alchemical process</note>. Through these four works, nature is turned from below, so that all the material of our Stone remains at the bottom of the glass, and nothing volatile rises anymore, but everything remains fixed <note>resistant to the heat of the fire</note>. Thus, with these four principal works, you have completed our Stone or the Work of Nature.

->Raymond Lully<-
<note>Raimundus Lullius, a Majorcan polymath whose name was frequently invoked in alchemical literature to provide authority to the text</note>

(k) Therefore, pour water over its earth <unclear>m</unclear> and mix it by grinding immediately, soaking it <term>imbibing</term> <note>The process of adding liquid to a dry substance until it is fully absorbed</note> little by little, boiling it <term>decocting</term> weekly, and afterwards gently calcining it <note>heating to a high temperature to reduce the substance to powder</note>, until the earth drinks a fiftieth part of its own water. Beware, however, that you do not soak the earth except little by little, and with long grinding, after the drying of the earth: boil it by roasting only as much as the dissolution requires by soaking.

# ->P A N D O R A ,<-

Men devoted to earthly delights desire earthly delights above all else, and they omit no work or labor to acquire them, according to that saying of the eminent prophet Virgil: 
> To what do you not drive the hearts of men, 
> O cursed hunger for gold! 
<note>original: *Quid non mortalia pectora cogis / Auri sacra fames*. From Virgil’s *Aeneid*, Book 3. Here, "sacra" carries the archaic sense of "accused" or "monstrous."</note>

Because all men seek pleasures, and in order to truly be able to live as well and blessedly as they can, almost all the delights of this world can be obtained primarily through riches—according to that common proverb: **All things obey money.** <note>original: *Pecuniæ obediunt omnia*. A common Latin maxim derived from Ecclesiastes 10:19.</note> And the Philosopher <note>A standard medieval reference to Aristotle.</note> says in the fifth book of his *Ethics*: **Money was invented for this purpose, to serve as a kind of guarantor for obtaining whatever a man might wish.** 

Furthermore, the greatest riches are promised through the mastery of <term>this art</term> <note>Referring to alchemy, the "Great Work" of transmuting base metals into gold.</note>, namely true gold and true silver, and both in great quantity without great labor, from which coins may be fashioned through which all things may be possessed. Therefore, men—both the learned and the ignorant—easily believe in it; they strive for it by experimentation and attempt to acquire it through trial. 

There are, however, few who reach the truth of the art through their labor. The chief cause of this has been explained before: namely, the ignorance of secrets and negligence in study. There is also a specific twofold reason for this: first, **metaphorical speech.** 

Avicenna <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), a Persian polymath whose works on medicine and alchemy were foundational in the West.</note> says: **I have considered the books of those who affirm this art, and I found them void of the reasons or logical arguments that exist in every other art; I found that most of what is contained in them is similar to alienation—that is, metaphorical.**

<summary>This page explores the human drive for wealth through alchemy, citing Virgil and Aristotle, while explaining that the cryptic, metaphorical language of alchemical texts (as noted by Avicenna) prevents most from succeeding.</summary>

...or similitudes; but when I returned myself to natural principles, I then knew the art to be true. The second cause is the mixing of false things with true ones. Regarding this, Arnaldus <note>Arnaldus de Villa Nova (c. 1240–1311), a famous physician and alchemist.</note> says in his testament: "The philosophers have placed two modes in their books: one true and the other false." They placed the truth in obscure words so that it could not be understood except by the **sons of doctrine** <note>original: *filiis doctrinae*. A term for initiated students of alchemy who possess the spiritual or intellectual maturity to understand the work.</note>, so that a profane way of acting would not be given to the impious. They placed the false, however, under easily understood words, and this is what is commonly followed by those who work with <term>Mercury</term> <note>In alchemy, Mercury represents the fluidic, transformative principle of matter.</note>, <term>Sulfur</term> <note>Representing the active, combustible, and masculine principle.</note>, <term>Arsenic</term>, and even in the metallic bodies themselves, and they find nothing. 

There are, therefore, very many who labor in this art in vain: because they can neither find the necessary things through their own wit, nor can they understand and extract the truth from the opinions of others. For they either err in the required matter <note>The "matter" refers to the starting material or "First Matter" (*Prima Materia*) needed for the Great Work.</note>, or in an unsuitable operation. Therefore, such people should be advised either to stay their hands from the work, or to read books more diligently and strive to understand more fully what they have read. Hence it is said in the *Book of Saturn*: "The philosophers did not write their books except for their sons; and I call those their 'sons' who perfectly understand their sayings, and not according to the letter." For operation according to the literal intention of the writing is a dissipation of riches and a waste of time.

<meta>This page continues the technical discussion on the interaction of elemental qualities (Heat, Cold, Moisture, Dryness) from page 647. The previous page established that elements must be reduced to their simple states; this page explains the mechanics of how these qualities either resist or assist one another in alchemical transformation.</meta>

-># PANDORA,<-

Opposite things are not joined together except through a medium <note>original: *medium*; an intermediate substance or quality that shares characteristics with two extremes, allowing them to unite</note>. **Heat** is the opposite of **cold**, and **moisture** is the opposite of **dryness**; therefore, neither of these is joined to the other except through a medium. Thus, that which is not contrary is inherently capable of unifying: so **heat** and **dryness** are joined by their own nature, since they are in no way contrary to one another, and therefore from them results the **element of air** <note>In most Aristotelian systems, Hot + Dry equals Fire, but this text assigns them to Air.</note>. Likewise, **cold** and **dryness** are not contrary when joined, from which the **element of earth** is generated; nor are **cold** and **moisture** contrary, from which the **element of water** is gathered. 

But **heat** and **cold** are not joined together except through a medium—namely, through **moisture** and **dryness**—because they refuse to stand together, as one blunts <note>original: *obtundat*; to dull, deaden, or neutralize</note> the other due to their opposition. Therefore, **heat** and **cold** gather and disperse things of the same kind <note>original: *unigenea*</note> by dissolving and coagulating <note>original: *coagulando*; the process of thickening or becoming solid</note>, but **moisture** and **dryness** are gathered and dispersed by binding and moistening. Furthermore, simple generation and natural transformation is the operation of the elements; for **heat** and **cold** produce results when they overcome matter. However, when the active forces are overcome, the substances melt, because a partial violence and "indigestion" <note>original: *indigestio*; in alchemy, this refers to the failure of the "internal heat" to properly ripen or transform the matter</note> occurs. Wherefore it is clear that all universal things are changeable through **heat** and **cold**, and are simply generated and naturally transformed.

...stony and two are aquatic. The <term>stony</term> <note>original: *lapidea*</note> elements are fire and earth; the <term>aquatic</term> <note>original: *aquatica*</note> are truly air and water. You shall extract water from the moist substance, but air and fire from the dry substance. Regarding the earth, you should not worry about what substance it comes from, provided it is <term>fixed</term> <note>original: *fixa*; stable and resistant to heat</note>, for earth and fire "drink" the air, drying it and fixing it; conversely, water and air wash the earth and fire, <term>tinting</term> <note>original: *tingunt*; the process of changing the color and quality of a metal</note> and perfecting them. 

For this reason, it is necessary to have much water and much <term>oil</term> <note>original: *oleum*; here referring to a concentrated liquid essence or "sulfur"</note>, because the quantity of the **tincture** will be as great as the quantity of the oil. Therefore, the **stone** is gradually dissolved so that it may be converted into **Mercury**, and divided into the four elements so that its <term>First Matter</term> <note>original: *materia prima*; the original, undifferentiated substance of the universe</note> may be obtained entirely.

Next, it is washed so that its impurities are removed, and it returns to the color of **quicksilver** <note>original: *argenti vivi*; liquid mercury</note>, just as it was in the beginning, and the saltiness of its **sulfur** is diminished. Afterward, it is <term>calcined</term> <note>original: *calcinatur*; reduced to powder through high heat</note> so that its matter may be refined, allowing it to be converted from coarse to fine, and from thick to <term>subtle</term> <note>original: *subtile*; refined or spiritualized</note>. Then it is washed with the "water of Mercury" so that it may recover the moisture it lost during the calcination process.

From there, it is <term>sublimated</term> <note>original: *sublimatur*; vaporized and solidified to purify the substance</note> so that its refined matter may be further purified. All this refined material—the clean **sulfur** and **quicksilver**—is then held above the earth, made from the same substance from which gold and silver are naturally produced beneath the earth. Then, a <term>ferment</term> <note>original: *fermentum*; a substance that acts like a "yeast" to direct the transformation</note> is added from the material we wish to create: if we want gold, we add gold; if silver, silver. Finally, it is <term>incerated</term> <note>original: *inceratur*; softened with "oil" or "wax" to make it flowable</note> so that the spirit may be joined with the body and <term>fixed</term> <note>original: *figatur*; made stable and non-volatile</note> within it, until they become one.

PANDORA,

(ooo) But moving further with the matter / now consider only the **Weight** (*Pondus*), for I believe much depends on this / because a very specific measure must be observed in your joining together of the philosophers’ liquid essence / the ancient Arabs write of this thus: *The weight of the male shall always be singular, and of the female plural.* <note>original Latin: "Pondus Masculi singulare & fœminæ plurale semper esto." This refers to the specific ratio—often 1 to 2 or 1 to 3—of the active "male" substance to the passive "female" substance.</note> So that the woman does not dominate the man / nor the man be too powerful over the woman / and the <term>dissolving water <note>original: "Aqua resolvens"; the alchemical solvent used to break down the materials into their primary state.</note></term> must not be too deep / so that the seed or the sperm does not drown / *let there be unity through quality in the Trinity*, says Paracelsus <note>original: "sit unitas per qualitatem in Trinitate." Paracelsus was a famous 16th-century Swiss physician and alchemist who emphasized the "tria prima" (salt, sulfur, and mercury).</note>. In that parable there, it is quite finely indicated by the mill-wheels and their number, representing the **Proportion of Mercury to Sulfur** <note>original: "Proportio Mercurii ad Sulphur."</note>: while under the mill-water, the <term>solvent <note>original: "Menstruum"; in alchemy, this is a specialized solvent, often called the "philosophical vinegar," used to dissolve solids.</note></term> is hidden—and yet clearly revealed.

### Or God’s Noblest Gift.

...in this place. Everything born has its own proper time: all fruits and plants are at their best when they are mature; likewise **Our Stone** <note>original Latin: "Lapis noster"; the Philosopher's Stone, the goal of the alchemical process.</note> is better for two reasons: first, because of the time—namely, when it is born in the spring. Other things, like <term>gum <note>original: "gummi"; in alchemy, this refers to a thick, resinous, or "sticky" substance extracted from the matter, often representing the "clinging" quality of the soul of the metal.</note></term>, are changed and flow out with the summer heat; but Our Gum is best poured out in the springtime. For it most closely approaches the nature of human blood and the generation of animals: blood increases most in the spring, when animals are incited to mate and birds to nest. Therefore, the matter of our Stone must be chosen then, and applied most conveniently to the work at that time, so that our **flying bird** <note>original: "avis noster volans"; an alchemical metaphor for a substance that has been made volatile or "spiritualized" through heat.</note> may be produced, whether feathered or unfeathered.

Wherefore Raymond <note>likely referring to Raymond Lull, a 13th-century philosopher and supposed alchemist.</note> says regarding these terms: *Let the Stone be placed in the physical vessel at the beginning of spring, with the sun being in Aries.* <note>original Latin: "Ponatur autem Lapis in vase physico in principio veris sole existente in Ariete." Aries, the Ram, marks the start of the astrological year in March.</note> For at this time, as Raymond of Marseilles <note>a 12th-century astronomer and scholar.</note> says, heat and humidity increase more, as do blood and <term>yellow bile <note>original: "cholera"; one of the four bodily humors, associated with heat and dryness.</note></term> together. 

And for this reason, this element of the Stone also abounds more in the spring; in this way, nature assists art, time assists the work, and the plants assist the <term>Mastery <note>original: "magisterium"; the completed alchemical process or the "great work" itself.</note></term>. Second, it is better because of the freshness of the fruit: fresh things are better than old ones, provided they are mature. For anything generated from individual things, once torn from its roots, is gradually drawn out more mildly until it is totally corrupted. Our Stone, however, is most tender, and its virtue quickly evaporates unless it is nourished by our heat. Therefore, an old or "aged" substance is not suitable for our work, just as...

(pp) For this reason, the matter must be converted so many times from one nature into another, in order to perform all those things that are in its governance, so as to lead it to perfection. This is why the **Sages** <note>original Latin: "Sapientes"; the ancient and medieval masters of alchemy.</note> bestowed many names upon the Stone; after they had dissolved the matter of the Stone and made it spiritual, they said the matter was a **vile thing** <note>original: "rem vilem"; alchemists often claimed the secret ingredient was something common or "worthless" found in nature to deter the uninitiated.</note>. And when they had sublimated it, they called it a **Serpent** and a **venomous beast**. When they had calcined it <note>reduced it to a powder through heat.</note>, they said it was **salt**, and things of this sort. And when they had dissolved it, they called it **water**, and said it could be found in all places. When they had reduced it to **oil**, they called the matter a **viscous thing** <note>thick or sticky.</note>, and said it was for sale everywhere. Yet when they had congealed it, they named it **earth**, and said that both the poor and the rich possessed it. And when they had clothed it in whiteness, they called it **virgins' milk** <note>original Latin: "lac virginum"; a common alchemical term for a white, liquid mercurial substance.</note>, and a "white thing." And when they had sublimated its redness upward, they called it **fire**, and a "red thing." And in this way, just as the matter of the Stone was converted into a specific nature, they bestowed a name upon it, until it was brought to its final end.

*M. Johannes Isaac.* <note>Likely referring to Johannes Isaac Hollandus, a celebrated Dutch alchemist whose works were highly influential in the late Middle Ages.</note>

## *Treatise of Lord Thomas Aquinas*

(aa) But truly, truly, many **pseudo-philosophers** <note>original: *pseudo-philosophi*; refers to charlatans or "puffers" who claimed to be alchemists but lacked true understanding.</note> will come after me, who will lead practitioners astray; I find only two types of such men who obscure this science. The first is ignorant of the art and a **sophist** <note>In this context, a "sophist" is a deceiver who uses clever but false arguments to trick people out of their money.</note>: the second is indeed knowledgeable, but an **envious Philosopher**. The first composes deceptive books, bearing witness to his own deceptions and tricks, and he writes at the head of these works the names of great **Philosophers**, so that they might appear to contain the true art and the **perfect elixir** <note>The "elixir" was the sought-after substance capable of transmuting base metals into gold or curing all diseases.</note>. And so that they may be more easily believed by men, they carry about powders of stones, either white or red <note>These colors refer to the *albedo* (whiteness) and *rubedo* (redness), the final stages of the alchemical Great Work.</note>, and they handle gold and silver; but those who follow them fail in their operations when they put those writings to the test. 

The second type is entirely envious; he has composed books on those things which are most remote from the truth, in order to lead men away from the true path as much as he can. He strives to prove his sayings through reasonings alone, which seem most certain to the foolish: he places the art in herbs, and the fruits of plants, and in many foreign and remote vegetables. Or, so that he might seem to be leaving us the true art, he speaks more "philosophically," basing his foundation upon the **four elements**, which are the true materials of Philosophy; yet he extracts them from many things, such as from vegetables, and animals, and from many other foreign sources, namely—

(c) Let the **practitioner** <note>original Latin: *Artifex*; referring to the alchemist as a skilled craftsman of nature.</note> be prudent, and possess a naturally subtle and profound intellect, and excel in excellent judgment. Moreover, let him be learned, so that whatever he does not achieve through natural wit, this deficiency may be remedied through study. For whoever wishes to reach this science, says **Arnaldus** <note>Arnaldus de Villa Nova (c. 1240–1311), a famous physician and alchemist.</note>, and is not a philosopher, is a fool: because this science is concerned only with the secrets of the Philosophers. Let him be industrious and hardworking, and of a constant will. For in this business, if the difficulty of the work and tedious fatigue make the worker negligent, it deprives him of the expected joy, suffocates hope, and destroys effectiveness. Let him not be prone to anger, but patient and long-suffering. For haste, says **Geber** <note>An Arabic alchemist (Jabir ibn Hayyan), though often referring to the Latin "Pseudo-Geber," whose works were foundational to Western alchemy.</note>, is from the father, the devil <note>original Latin: *Festinatio enim... à patre diabolo est.*</note>. Let him be of his own independent judgment and free, not distracted by other cares or business. Likewise, let him be especially tenacious of the **secret** <note>original Latin: *Secreti... tenax*; referring to the vow of silence or Hermetic secrecy.</note>, lest he bring danger upon himself or provide an opportunity for wrongdoing to others. Let him be neither a spendthrift nor a miser, yet sufficiently wealthy, and let him possess a great abundance of books.

->Master Valentine.<- <note>Basil Valentine, the legendary 15th-century Benedictine monk and alchemist credited with many discoveries in antimony and mineral acids.</note>

The alchemist took other **Mercury** once more, put it into the glass again, and guarded it diligently so that his wife could not get to it or touch it. But the quicksilver flew out through the chimney again.

In this state, the **alchemist** <note>original: *Alchymist*</note> reflects that the **First Matter** <term>The *Prima Materia*, the foundational, formless substance that alchemists believed was necessary to create the Philosopher's Stone.</term> of the **Stone** must be volatile. In that sleep, an **old man** appeared to him, greeted him, and said: "Friend, why do you mourn and trouble yourself?" But he said: "I would like to make the **Philosophical Stone**." Whereupon the old man asked: "Friend, out of what do you wish to make it?"

**Alchemist:** "Out of quicksilver or **Mercury**."

# Or the Noblest Gift of God.

The Old Man: Indeed, what kind of **Mercury**?
**Alchemist:** There is surely no more than one.
The Old Man: It is true, nevertheless, that there is only one **Mercury**; but the same is distributed into many kinds, and one part of it is purer than the others.
**Alchemist:** O Lord, I have skill enough to purify it in the very best way, with vinegar, saltpeter, and vitriol <term>Vitriol: a historical term for sulfate minerals, often used as powerful corrosive agents in alchemical reactions.</term>.
The Old Man: Believe me, that is not the right purification, nor is this the right, true **Mercury**. The ancient Sages and Philosophers have another quicksilver and **Mercury**, and another purification—and with that, the old man vanished.

->*Michael Sendivogius.*<- <note>Sendivogius (1566–1636) was a famous Polish alchemist and philosopher, renowned for his theories on the "food of life" found in the air.</note>

This is now the right beginning of this art: for all metals have their origin in **Mercury** <note>original: *Mercurio*</note>. Therefore, if one wishes to turn them into **the Sun** <note>original: *Solem*</note>: that is, gold, or into **the Moon** <note>original: *Lunam*</note>: that is, silver, then a medicine must first be made from **the Sun** or **the Moon** as if from their origin: that is, **Mercury**. # PANDORA,

...produced by both nature and art: but by the former effectively and principally, and by the latter instrumentally and organically. Thus, alchemists first thoroughly purify the matter of <term>quicksilver</term> <note>original: "arg. vivi" (argentum vivum), or mercury.</note> and sulfur, which are implanted in all metals, and combine them. Then, they lead forth the elementary and celestial <term>virtues</term> <note>In this context, "virtues" are the inherent powers or spiritual qualities of a substance.</note> inherent in such matter to the proportion of the metallic mixture they intend to bring about. At that point, nature itself operates, and not art—except by helping organically and by stripping away [impurities], as we have said. In this way, they are seen to draw out and create true gold and silver. 

For what the elementary and celestial powers do in natural vessels <note>The "natural vessels" refer to the cavities within the earth where metals grow over long periods.</note>, they also do in artificial vessels <note>Laboratory glassware such as flasks or retorts.</note>, provided the artificial ones are shaped after the manner of the natural ones. What nature achieves through the heat of the sun and the stars, art will achieve through the heat of fire: so long as it is tempered in such a way that it does not exceed the self-moving and <term>informing power</term> <note>The "informing power" is the active principle that gives a substance its specific identity (its "form").</note> that resides within the metals. 

For there is a celestial power within, which first mixed the matter, and it is inclined toward this or that [form] through the assistance of art. Alchemy, therefore, proceeds in this manner: that is, by breaking down one thing, removing it from its <term>species</term> <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, the "species" is the essential nature of a thing, like being "lead" as opposed to "gold."</note>, and—with the help of those things already within the matter—introducing the species of another. 

Therefore, of all alchemical operations, the best is that which proceeds from the very same things from which nature proceeds—such as the purification of sulfur through <term>decoction</term> <note>The process of boiling a substance to extract its essence.</note> and <term>sublimation</term> <note>A process where a solid is heated into a gas and then cools back into a solid, used to purify substances.</note>, and the purification of quicksilver, and the proper mixing of these with the matter of the metal. # THE NOBLEST GIFT OF GOD.

Now, my son, our discourse shall be regarding the great works which our ancestors performed for us. You should know, my son, that they labored in the **Art** <note>The "Art" refers to Alchemy, often called the "Sacred Art" or "Hermetic Art."</note> in various ways, and yet they all arrived at one and the same goal; however, their **stone** <note>original: *lapis*. The Philosopher’s Stone, the goal of the alchemical work.</note> did not perform an equally great **projection** <note>original: *projectionem*. The final act of alchemical transformation where a small amount of the "Stone" is thrown onto base metal to transmute it into gold or silver.</note>: one achieved a high degree, another a long-lasting one, according to whether they made their works sharp or of a deep color. Some sweated for a long time before they produced the stone: others, by the sharpness of their wit, shortened the time—as is now done daily—through much sweat and labor. And among our ancestors, some labored for three years, others for four, before they produced the stone. For in those times, **strong water** <term>aqua fortis</term> <note>original: *aqua fortis*. Historically, this refers to nitric acid, a powerful solvent that allowed alchemists to dissolve metals much faster than earlier methods.</note> was unknown, and they used nothing but **distilled vinegar**. Now their descendants have discovered strong waters, which has greatly shortened the work. 

And you shall understand, my son, that the work can easily be shortened; in the first preparation let the matter be made **subtle** <note>Refined or ground down to its most essential, pure state.</note>, so that the components may be properly united, so that nature alone does not have the task of **digesting** <note>original: *concoquere*. An alchemical term for "cooking" or maturing a substance through steady heat, mimicking natural processes.</note> it, and let the moist be so subtly mixed with the dry that it becomes one single thing, so that the **soul** is united to the **body** and the **spirit** in such a way that they are one. For this reason, **Hermes** our Philosopher <note>Referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of alchemy.</note> says: "In the beginning of your works, do not be slow in properly cleansing and clarifying all things, so that you may later rejoice." **Geber**, **Dantynus**, and **Morienus** <note>Three famous alchemical authorities: Geber (Jabir ibn Hayyan), John Dastin (likely "Dantynus"), and Morienus Romanus.</note> also say: "Join the water properly with the earth, and the moist with the dry, so that afterward you may see the **blackness of the sea** <note>original: *maris nigredinem*. A poetic reference to the "nigredo" or black stage of alchemy.</note>, that is, its dark color, which is seen during its **putrefaction** <note>The stage of decomposition or "rotting" of the matter, which alchemists believed was necessary for rebirth and transformation.</note>..."

And these two preparations are made together in this way: Take two pounds of <term>saltpeter: original: "salis petræ"; a mineral salt used as a powerful oxidizing agent.</term> and Roman vitriol, and grind them finely, and by stirring them in an iron pan, dry them over a somewhat slow fire, so that the moisture of the water may evaporate. # PANDORA, #

The third degree of fire should be increased once more, immediately after the final **putrefaction** <note>original: "putrefaction"; the stage of decomposition where the matter turns black</note>, once the **male and female seeds** <note>alchemical metaphors for the active (sulfur) and passive (mercury) principles</note> have been mixed together. And you say: "Now it works," and that is true,

In truth I do not mislead you:
Outside of the beautiful <term>medicine: original "Artzney," here referring to the alchemical elixir or the Great Work.</term>

Just as I wish to show the way herein.
Worse than all this

So that I know how or what
Exists within these two <term>faculties: original "Facultäten," here meaning the specific disciplines or fields of alchemy and magic.</term>,

Time and curiosity <note>The author uses "Fürwitz," which implies an over-eager or prying curiosity into forbidden things.</note> brought this about,

# P A N D O R A ,

If you wish to hide the same, you may call it the <term>fifth essence</term> <note>original: *quintam essentiam*. In alchemy and early natural philosophy, this is the "quintessence," a pure, incorruptible substance distinct from the four earthly elements of fire, air, water, and earth.</note>, the fifth being. For it has its own nature, and the philosophers did not wish to reveal this name of theirs to anyone, but rather chose to let the truth be buried with them. (e)

<margin>(e) Therefore, only the unwise person—who has never sensed the path of true <term>medicine</term> <note>original: *Medicin*</note>—mocks it. For mockers do not have enough [insight] from this to recognize such a root and noble medicine which heals all diseases.</margin>

Blessed is the person to whom God gives the time and the life to arrive at this high being, regardless of whether they may be old. For <term>Geber</term> <note>Jabir ibn Hayyan (c. 721–c. 815), a foundational figure in early chemistry and alchemy whose Latinized name was "Geber."</note> says that although the philosophers who possessed it were old, they nevertheless delighted themselves with it in their old days. In this way it happens that all things influencing life, as celestial things, incline downwards through the mediation of air, while all things that have obtained life strive upwards in turn by a certain instinct and desire for higher things toward those very stars; inasmuch as from where they originated, they shall abundantly receive their strength, grow, and be perfected by them.

### Or God’s Noblest Gift.

According to the doctrine of the ancient Egyptian astrologers, nothing is produced on the earth or in the water that was not first sown there from the heavens. The heavens act like a farmer who carries out the cultivation; they instill their heat into the earth and, through an effective influence, lead everything to perfect and complete maturity. This is also confirmed by **Aristotle** in his books *On Generation and Corruption* <note>original: "de Ortu & interitu"</note>. 

The lower fire, however, has the base of its pyramid fixed to the earth and presents one of the six faces of a cube. The **Pythagoreans** <note>followers of the philosopher Pythagoras, who associated geometric shapes with the elements</note> attributed this shape to it because of its stable form and unchanging stability. From the sharp tip of this lower fire, subtle vapors are carried upward, which serve as nourishment for the sun and other celestial bodies, as **Phurnutus** <note>Lucius Annaeus Cornutus, a Stoic philosopher of the 1st century AD</note> writes along with others. To **Vesta** <note>the Roman goddess of the hearth and sacred fire</note>, he says, "inextinguishable fire is attributed," perhaps because the power of the fire that exists in the world takes its nourishment from there, and because the sun subsists through her. 

This is exactly what **Hermes** says in his **Emerald Tablet** <note>original: "tabula smaragdina," a foundational text of alchemy and Hermetic philosophy</note>: "That which is below is like that which is above, and vice versa, to accomplish the miracles of the one thing."

# P A N D O R A,

Multiplication. Because that which is calcined <term>calcination</term> <note>The process of heating a substance to high temperatures to reduce it to a powder, removing impurities.</note> can be dissolved more easily than that which is uncalcined, it is necessary that the calcination and destruction of the sulfurous impurity and the combustible stench of the body go before. Also, whatever helpful waters or solvents <term>menstrua</term> <note>Alchemical solvents used to dissolve solids; the term likens the solvent's role to the life-giving fluids of a womb.</note> might be used must later be removed from it, leaving absolutely nothing foreign behind. This must be done with the most diligent care to prevent the stone's innermost generative and multiplicative power <note>original: "vis generativa & multiplicativa"</note> from being burned, destroyed, or driven away by external heat or other harmful accidents. Just as the Philosophers in the *Turba* <note>The *Turba Philosophorum*, or "Assembly of the Philosophers," is one of the oldest and most famous Latin alchemical texts, written as a record of a great gathering of sages.</note> highly warn against this in part 1, page 429:

> You should guard yourself most carefully during its purification and take heed against the loss of its power, so that the active virtue <note>original: "virtus activa"</note> is not smothered; for no seed grows or is increased if its generative power is taken away by external heat;

Once you have the seed <term>sperma</term> <note>Not used in a biological sense, but referring to the "metallic seed" or the concentrated essence of the matter being transformed.</note>, you can thereafter complete the entire work through gentle boiling. For first, we gather the seed from the magnesia <note>In alchemy, "magnesia" refers not to the modern chemical, but to a mysterious "prime matter" or crude mineral source from which the Stone's essence is extracted.</note>; we rot <term>putrefy</term> that which is gathered; we dissolve that which is rotted; we divide that which is dissolved; we purify that which is divided; we unite that which is purified; and thus the Work is fulfilled.

->Michael Sendivogius.<- <note>A famous Polish alchemist and physician (1566–1636) known for his theories on the "food of life" in the air (oxygen).</note>

### P A N D O R A ,

[Hot extraction] is that by which the subtle parts are separated from the coarse by descent through the medium of fire. This is why it is also called "distillation by descent." It is used in the preparation of pitch; when a pile of cut pine torches <note>original Latin: "tædarum concisarum"; resinous pine wood used for lighting and producing tar.</note> is made, with the air-holes closed up on all sides and a fire lit within the heap, the pitch flows downward. This can be seen in the works of Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder (23–79 AD), a Roman author of "Natural History."</note> (book 11, chapter 16) and Mattioli <note>Pietro Andrea Mattioli (1501–1577), a renowned Renaissance physician and botanist.</note>, who describe this operation exactly.

[Cold extraction] is that by which the separation of subtle parts from the thicker ones occurs through descent without the use of fire.

->Johann Beguin<- <note>Jean Beguin (c. 1550–1620) was a Flemish-born chemist and author of "Tyrocinium Chymicum," one of the first popular chemistry textbooks.</note>

Let this be thoroughly mixed with those things that are appropriate for it, as is written in the books of the philosophers <note>In alchemical literature, "philosophers" refers to the historical masters and authorities of the Art.</note>, and place upon it ignited

This is revealed and entrusted to Nature, for the Divine Will alone requires that His **great works** <note>original: *Magnalia*</note> be made known to those who place their strong hope in God, so that they may explore such high knowledge and working power. **Mars**. With **iron** <note>original: *Eysen*</note> it is fleeting <note>original: *flüchtig*; likely meaning the influence is unstable or the material is volatile during these times</note>.
**Mercury**. Working with **quicksilver** <note>original: *Quecksilber*</note> is good in Virgo and Gemini: and it is bad in Sagittarius and Pisces.

# Explanation of the First
## Author.

**A** The Tree comes from the seeds of the Man and the Woman <note>In alchemy, the "Man and Woman" represent the two primary principles, often Sulfur and Mercury, whose union begins the Great Work.</note>. When the seed has died in the earth, then it rises up, from which a tree grows, of unspeakable fruit and manifold operation <note>original: "Würckung." This refers to the *Arbor Philosophica* or Philosophical Tree, a symbol of the growing and maturing alchemical Stone.</note>.

->**B** Sun. &emsp; &emsp; **C** Moon.<-

**D** The birds are the Sun’s seed and fly through the mountain of the Moon up into the heights of heaven, and bite into their own plumage, and return naked into the mountain again and die there a white death <note>The "white death" refers to the *Albedo* or "Whiteness" stage, where the matter is purified and fixed after its initial dissolution.</note>.

**E** The birds are the Moon’s seed and fly through the mountain of their father and mother up into the heights of the heavens, and take the radiance of the Sun, and thereby they become clear <note>original: "klar." Likely meaning transparent, bright, or purified.</note>, and fall back into the mountain again, and die there a black death <note>The "black death" refers to the *Nigredo* or "Blackness" stage, representing the putrefaction or decomposition necessary for rebirth.</note>.

**F** Distillatory <term>Distillatorium</term> <note>A vessel or apparatus used for distillation, the process of vaporizing and condensing a substance to purify it.</note> of the Sun.
**G** Distillatory of the Moon.

# Or the Noblest Gift of God.

Plato's daughter calls out and writes thus: protect me, and I will protect you; grant me my right, so that I may help you, my son. My streams are deep within me; Luna <note>The Moon, representing silver or the feminine, receptive principle in alchemy</note> is truly mine, and my light surpasses all light. My goodness is the highest and noblest of all goodness—to be enjoyed and well-increased. I bring forth the light, but darkness is in my nature, unless my metal becomes dry. (a)

(a) This blessed water <note>original: "gebenedeyte Wasser"</note> is called the Daughter of Plato by the Philosophers <note>Alchemists often referred to themselves as "Philosophers"</note>; she has power and authority over all treasures.

->*The Sophic Knot Untied.*<-

# P A N D O R A ,

<margin>(d) But although many and infinite works of this kind are imagined by the Philosophers, yet there is only one true work, which, consisting solely of an equal and tempered mixing of the elements, is firm and fixed. For this reason, it is also the greatest aid to health, and no less a remedy for poverty. Moreover, it is founded in the **earth of gold**, which is deservedly called Isir <note>original Latin: *Iſir*, an alchemical term likely derived from the Arabic *al-iksir*, or Elixir</note>, or the Elixir, or the <term>ferment <note>original: *fermentum*. In alchemy, this is a substance—like yeast in bread—added to a base material to "leaven" it, transforming its nature and multiplying its power.</note></term> of the Philosophers.</margin>

**However, we warned a little above that this ferment is twofold: namely, of the Sun <note>representing Gold</note> and of the Moon <note>representing Silver</note>.**

By the "ferment of the Sun" is understood the seed of the male; and by the "ferment of the Moon" the seed of the female. From these, first comes the conjunction <note>chemical union</note>, and afterwards a true and chaste generation. The ferment of gold is gold, just as the leaven of bread is bread. And just as in the making of bread a little leaven raises and ferments a great quantity of dough, so also that little bit of "earth" which this stone contains is sufficient for the nourishment of the whole stone.

Whence **Avicenna** <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), a Persian polymath whose works on medicine and chemistry were foundational to Western alchemy</note> says: "Leaven reduces that which is added to it to its own nature, color, and flavor in every way—namely, from potentiality into act. For it whitens the preparation, or rather multiplies it; it strengthens its spirituality, annihilates combustion <note>prevents the substance from being destroyed or "burnt" by the fire</note>, and contains the <term>tincture <note>the concentrated essence or coloring principle that allows the Stone to transmute other metals</note></term> so that it does not flee. It lightens bodies and makes them enter and join one another, which is the end of the work, without which the **Elixir** is not completed—just as dough is not leavened without leaven. This is why it is called the 'leaven of leaven' and the 'curd of curd.' For it does not only ferment the body..."

And thus you have created and brought into the world the Queen of Honors and the first newborn daughter of the **Philosophers** <note>Alchemists often referred to themselves as "Philosophers," meaning lovers of wisdom who study the secrets of nature.</note>, which, according to its perfection, is called the white <term>Elixir</term> <note>The "white elixir" is a substance capable of transmuting base metals into silver and represents the penultimate stage of the alchemical work.</note>, about which all books are filled with writing.

Therefore, you are rightly to be preferred above them, while they sit at the bottom in shame and mockery and remain in the darkness of misunderstanding until the enlightenment of nature follows afterward.

# Or God's Most Noble Gift.

The earth <term>Erdtreich: the domain of the soil and the subterranean world</term> is the mother of metals, and heaven is their father, according to the opinion of Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure to whom the foundations of alchemy and "Hermetic" philosophy are attributed</note>; and the earth is still pregnant with them in mountains, fields, plains, waters, and all other places. (a)

---

(a) It brings the greatest toil that a man can experience in mining to haul up and extract from the mine the stones, sand, and all the filth that is of no use, so that one may dig deeper. Up here on the surface, this is called rubble; in ships, it is called ballast. Now, it is a small expense to dissolve and separate it with an etching water <term>Etz-Wasser: a corrosive acid or "aqua fortis" used in metallurgy to separate precious metals from base ores</term>; it does not cost much if one proceeds correctly, by first washing away that which is lightest. When that is gone, the rest is easily managed. For one must not look at the earth as if it were mere grass; there is actually very little "earth" within the earth. Rather, all sorts of things are found within it, such as salt, juices <note>Early modern scientists often referred to liquid mineral substances as "juices" or "humors" of the earth</note>, wax, minerals <note>original: *mineralia*</note>, and stones. The earth is the least part of it, and yet the most noble, for it is the body <note>original: *Corpus*</note>.

(aa) If the earth (as certain imaginative theorists—most notably Aristotle—believe) were the mother of metals, the matter would be straightforward: for in that case, the falling seed would soon return to its origin, or reach the Mercurial veins into which it would sow itself and rise anew. For just as a plant cannot grow without earth from air alone, so also metal cannot grow from earth alone or from common quicksilver <note>original: *argento vivo vulgari*; mercury in its base, liquid form</note>, even if wagonloads full of it were sown in the earth—a fact which daily experience abundantly testifies.

It usually happens, however, that sometimes the falling rays of the stars (provided they are of one and the same nature) mix with metals, stones, and minerals that have fallen from their highest state <note>This refers to minerals that have been "degraded" or separated from their pure elemental source</note>. These figures introduce themselves through that celestial influence and receive a "signature" from nature. Hence it is that various figures are found upon stones, wood, metals, and gems; these are often esteemed as worthless, yet there is no such figure that does not have its own unique demonstration and power, which is worth noting. ## On Philosophical Nitre.

This must be purified to the highest degree through the boiling of the stone, filtration, evaporation, and coagulation, so that through the Art it attains such transparency that it even surpasses crystal.

Once this is done, the dead earth <note>original: "todte Erden"; referring to the *caput mortuum*, the useless solid residue left over after a chemical process.</note> from which this crystalline salt was leached must be <term>calcined</term> <note>A process of heating a substance to high temperatures in air to achieve decomposition or oxidation.</note> with the highest degree of fire. Take four and a half pounds of the previously calcined earth and distill it according to the Art using a <term>retort</term> <note>A glassware vessel with a long, downward-pointing neck used for distilling substances.</note> into a large <term>receiver</term> <note>A vessel designed to collect the liquid (distillate) produced during the process.</note> into which two pounds of spring water have been poured. Distill according to the degrees [of heat] until the drops are <term>precipitated</term> into the water like little sparks. Ensure the joints are well <term>luted</term> <note>original: "anlutiret"; sealed with an airtight paste or clay to prevent the escape of volatile vapors.</note> so that nothing escapes as vapor. When a distillation is finished, the furnace must be allowed to become completely cold before the receiver is removed. Repeat these distillations as many times as necessary until a sufficient amount of the material is obtained.

(bbb bb) **Mercury** is moist and warm; in this, it agrees with the **Air**. And although **Mercury** is the weightiest **star** <note>original: *Astrum*; in alchemical philosophy, metals were often referred to as "terrestrial stars" linked to planetary influences.</note>, it nonetheless desires to be the lightest of all and to escape the burning **Fire**, to rise above, and to resolve itself into another **element** <note>original: *Elementum*</note>, namely into **air** <note>original: *nempè in aërem*</note>. Thus, it remains rightly compared to the **Air**; for just as **Sulphur** is understood through **Fire**, so too must the **Air** be understood through **Nitre** <note>Saltpeter</note>, and vice versa. This is because in **Mercury**, two elements—namely **Fire** and **Air**—are most clearly and evidently found; and both are cold on the outside, but fiery and hot on the inside.

(aa) All who have written about the **seed of the metals** are in agreement on this: they say that the male seed of the metal is **Sulfur**, and the female is ***Mercury***. This, however, must be understood according to its proper meaning and not be mistaken for common sulfur and *mercury*. For visible *metallic mercury* <note>original: "Mercurius metallum."</note> is a body in its own right, one of the seven bodies <note>The seven metals: Gold, Silver, Mercury, Copper, Iron, Tin, and Lead.</note>; therefore, it cannot be a seed. Furthermore, it is cold, and coldness alone cannot be a seed. Likewise, sulfur is the food of the metal—how then can it be a seed? Indeed, the seed consumes the sulfur; how could one seed consume another? What kind of body would result from that? 

Therefore, it is a great error to understand it in the common sense. Rather, the seed of all **bodies** <note>In this context, "bodies" refers to the solid metals.</note> is the **mercury of bodies** <note>original: "Mercurius corporum." This refers to the essential, "philosophical" mercury that alchemists believed was the root of all matter, distinct from the liquid metal found in a pharmacy.</note>, which by nature is the hottest of all. For this reason, when the **mercury of bodies** is engaged in a Work and has enough food, six **Mercuries** always drive forth one body, whichever one of the six it may be, depending on whether they are in the ascending or descending phase.

# Or the Noblest Gift of God

Others—whenever they, through their foolish purifications, treat **Mercury** in various ways: through <term>subliming</term> <note>original: "sublimiren." The process of heating a substance until it turns into a gas and then solidifies again, used to purify volatile materials.</note>, <term>precipitating</term> <note>original: "præcipitiren." Causing a solid substance to separate and settle out of a liquid solution.</note>, <term>calcining</term> <note>original: "calciniren." Reducing a metal to a powder or ash through the application of intense heat.</note> by hand until it becomes completely black, like soot or **lamp-black**; through distilling from special <term>dregs</term> <note>original: "Fæcibus." The sediment or waste material left over after a chemical process.</note> and then rubbing it with **wine vinegar**; through calcining with **strong waters** <note>original: "starcken Wassern." Historically, this refers to concentrated acids like nitric acid or aqua fortis.</note>; through countless washings; through transforming the **Mercury** into different forms and afterwards making it **living** <note>original: "lebendig." In alchemy, "living" mercury refers to the liquid, running state of the metal as opposed to a fixed powder.</note> again—through all these labors, they imagine that they certainly hold the secret of our **Mercury** in their hands, when in truth all these paths are merely deceptive. And the **Mercury** that is so poorly treated remains, after all, just the same previous **Mercury** as before.

Thus, they have struck themselves against this **rocky cliff** <note>original: "Stein-Fels." Used here as a metaphor for a massive obstacle or a "stumbling block" that prevents progress.</note> more than against any other thing, until they recognize how our **Mercury** is to be distinguished from the common kind, and our preparations from the common <term>sophistical</term> <note>original: "Sophistischen." Practices performed by those who lack the true philosophical understanding of alchemy, often resulting in "false" or purely superficial results.</note> ones, which have no equality to one another.

For our **Mercury** is essential and <term>radical</term> <note>original: "radicalisch." Meaning it pertains to the "root" (radix) or fundamental, inherent essence of the matter rather than just its surface appearance.</note> to our body and **participates** in its internal nature; and for that reason, it is said that it is the **Mercury** without which no being exists. ...physically distinguished through three **Principles** <note>original: "drey *Principia*." # Or the Noblest Gift of God.

Therefore *Theophrastus* <note>Theophrastus (c. 371 – c. 287 BC), a successor to Aristotle. ->**Metals**<-

The origin, birth, distinction, friendship, and enmity of metals must be well known and understood by anyone who wishes to achieve anything in this Art. <note>The "Art" is Alchemy. "Friendship and enmity" refers to what we now call chemical affinity—how certain substances naturally attract or repel one another.</note>

All metals grow from a single root, and their initial matter is of one kind. 5

Metals, how they are generated from Mercury and Sulfur. 85 <note>original: "Mercurio und sulphure." In alchemical theory, Mercury (the feminine, volatile principle) and Sulfur (the masculine, combustible principle) are the two parents of all metals.</note>

Rich metals are the perfect bodies, such as Gold and Silver; the poor are the imperfect metals, namely the five others. 95. 96 <note>The seven metals of antiquity were Gold, Silver, Copper, Iron, Tin, Lead, and Mercury. Here, Gold and Silver are "perfect" because they do not rust or perish in fire.</note>

Metals, how they are generated in the earth. 102

The matter of metals consists of three joined parts: a metallic Sulfur, which is heavenly; a metallic Mercury, which is spiritual; and a metallic Salt, which is bodily. 102 <note>This is the *Tria Prima* or "Three Primes" theory: everything is made of Soul (Sulfur), Spirit (Mercury), and Body (Salt).</note>

Metals are opened by minerals. 103 <term>Opened: To "open" a metal (aufgeschlossen) means to dissolve it or break its hard outer "lock" to release its internal virtues for medicine or transmutation.</term>

Metals and minerals have the same metallic seed. 112 <term>Metallic seed: original "sperma metallicum." Alchemists believed metals were living things that grew from seeds within the "womb" of the earth.</term>

The form of metals, and how they can be transformed. 132

The first essence of metal is Mercury. 132

The transformation of metals is easy and possible. 134

The nature of metals and ore is to be explored above all things. 298

Metals should not be dissolved simply so that one might thereafter make a metal from their mixture. 317 <note>original: "solvirt." This likely warns against mere alloying (mixing metals), which is not considered true alchemical transmutation.</note>

No metal is so pure that it does not also have its impurity. 317

### Index of Subjects and Words <note>original: *Index Rerum, & Verborum*</note>

**Two fires**, the philosophical and the common / 829 <note>Philosophical fire refers to the gentle, internal heat of the alchemical vessel, as opposed to the "common" heat of a furnace.</note>
**Two Mercuries**, 928 <note>Likely referring to the "fixed" and "volatile" states of the substance.</note>
**Two quicksilvers** of differing substance / but of one root / 942 <note>original: *Quecksilber*</note>
**Two-fold image** which is partly a man’s and partly a woman’s figure / like a **hermaphrodite** <note>original: *Zwydorn*; an archaic term describing a dual-natured being, often called a Rebis, symbolizing the union of opposites.</note> / that carries an **imperial scepter** in the hand / 908
**Two crowns** / 981
**Two waters** make one water. 987 <note>This refers to the alchemical process where two distinct solvents are combined to create a single, more potent "universal" solvent.</note>

# LEXICON OF ALCHEMY.
## BY JOHANNES MICHAEL FAUST,
### Doctor of Medicine and Permanent
### Physician of Frankfurt.

### A.

Abam } **Lead** <note>original Latin: *Plumbum*; German: *Bley*.</note>, also known as
Abartamen } Capricorn <note>In alchemical astrology, Capricorn is ruled by Saturn, which corresponds to Lead.</note>,
Aiarazat } Cleansed <note>original: *Castigatus*.</note>, Chibor, Duoplum,
Accib. } Draiccium, Elerator.

Araxat, Abusa Rub, Alech, Abonoç, Alabri, Alokot, Amiec, Amie, Amioch, Amitieh, Araxat, Azoro, Balamba, Cartistilium, Koal, Molybdos <note>The Greek term for lead.</note>, Mosquet dei, Molibra, Mofider, Rafas, Rafasa, Roles, Roc, Rocli. <note>This extensive list provides various synonyms for Lead, many derived from Arabic or corrupted Greek terms used in medieval manuscripts.</note>

Abesanum, *that is, wheel-clay.* <note>original: *lutum rotæ*; German: *Rad-Leym*. A mixture of clay and other materials (like horse dung or hair) used to seal alchemical vessels or "lute" them against high heat.</note>

Abessidum, *which is Rebis, namely the ultimate matter of foods:* The last remaining matter from the consumption and parching of food. <note>In this context, it refers to the waste products of digestion or the "excrement" of the chemical process.</note>

Abestus } **Quicklime** or **unslaked lime** <note>original: *calx non extincta* or *calx viva*; German: *ungelöschter oder lebendiger Kalch*. Used for its intense heat when reacting with water.</note>,
Abesum } also called Albesten, Abesten, Acmorago, or Asbestus.

Abicum, *that is, a cover* or a lid. <note>original German: *ein Deckel*.</note>

<meta>catchword: Abne</meta>

<summary>This opening page of the lexicon provides a variety of synonyms for common alchemical substances, focusing heavily on different names for Lead and materials used for sealing vessels, such as wheel-clay and quicklime.</summary>
